I. Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy was thrown under the bus often enough to know how much
it hurts. Wiser after the experience of the US abandoning him in arms supply as well as
withdrawing intelligence support in war, Mr Zelenskyy played the supplicant to perfection,
even abiding by a sartorial ceasefire as he came to the White House. The marked contrast
between the upbeat mood of Monday in Washington when Mr Zelenskyy came with the
physical and moral support of virtually the whole of Europe, EU and NATO and the insipid
one-sided nature of the Alaskan Trump-Putin meeting of Friday can be interpreted to imagine
there is a birth of hope towards the Ukraine war ending. Of course, it is still in Russian President
Vladimir Putin’s hands as he is the one holding all the cards after he impassively withstood
Trump’s charm offensive at the military base in Anchorage.

A bright positive to emerge from the summit of leaders of the “coalition of the willing” and Mr
Trump and Mr Zelenskyy was that there will be security guarantees for Ukraine, possibly even
American boots on the ground to ensure that any peace agreement is adhered to after more of
the Donbas region, which is not quite in control of Russian troops yet, is given away in
exchange for peace everywhere, beginning with Zaporizhzhia and Kherson. Mr Trump has
scuppered Ukrainian dreams of joining NATO, but American guarantees of security could
mean almost as much, as it could preclude Mr Putin from starting a war in the future, perhaps
at least so long as Mr Trump stays in the White House until January 2029. If a peace deal that
is elusive only due to Mr Putin’s intransigence is struck and Mr Zelenskyy delivers on his
promise of holding fresh elections, a rosy scenario can be envisaged.

All the theatre and the flattery appeared to pay off with the Europeans serving up a masterclass
in dealing with an egotistical Mr Trump. There may be something there for India as well since
it is left facing a huge Trump tariff trauma. But, if the war does stop, and Russia becomes an
acceptable entity for the Western world again, there may be relief for India that was not able to
find a way to tweak Mr Trump to its liking and advantage. Let the war end first.

II. "Throughout the 1970s, Italy was convulsed by a series of bomb attacks, political
kidnappings and assassinations" carried out by left-wing terrorists, said Ian Thomson in the FT.
Of the groups that operated during the anni di piombi ("years of lead"), the "most feared" was
the Brigate Rosse (Red Brigades), which "combined a Marxist-Leninist utopianism with a


murderous disregard for human life". During its "18-year reign of terror", the group killed
around 75 people and maimed hundreds. Its highest-profile victim was former prime minister
Aldo Moro, who was kidnapped in March 1978 and whose bullet-riddled body was found 55
days later in the boot of a Renault 4.

Now John Foot, a professor of history at Bristol University, has written a "grimly absorbing"
history of the brigatisti and their attempts to overthrow the Italian state. As his "superbly
researched" book shows, the group subjected Italy to "some of the bloodiest acts of terrorism
yet seen in an industrialised society" – all for nothing, as they never came close to realising
their goals. Their story, Foot observes, amounted to a "national tragedy". The Red Brigades
was founded in 1970 by Renato Curcio, a student in Trento, his girlfriend (later wife)
Margherita Cagol, and Alberto Franceschini, a communist from Reggio Emilia. "Its roots,
however, lay much deeper," said Simon Gaul in Literary Review – in disquiet at America's
influence over Italy, growing industrial unrest in the country's northern heartlands, and a belief
that neo-fascists were plotting a military coup.

At first, the Red Brigades was backed financially by Giangiacomo Feltrinelli, the "increasingly
activist publisher of 'The Leopard' and 'Doctor Zhivago'", said James Owen in The Times. But
that source dried up in 1972, when Feltrinelli blew himself up while trying to detonate an
electricity pylon outside Milan. Italy in the early 1970s had an "epidemic of kidnaps by
organised crime groups", and the brigatisti jumped on this bandwagon, said Simon Heffer in
The Daily Telegraph. They first targeted industrialists or minor officials, but widened their net
to include prominent politicians. And they upped the violence, adding kneecappings and
executions to their repertoire ("Strike One to Educate 100" became their mantra). Eventually,
it became clear the group were "killing just because they could" – and as public support seeped
away, they turned on each other, and finally disbanded in 1988. Based on exemplary
scholarship, Foot's book provides a "fascinating insight" into these "moronic" fanatics.

SOURCE: https://theweek.com/culture-life/books/the-red-brigades-history-book-review

III. Dry days - specific days when sale of alcohol is not allowed - is a custom peculiar to India
among countries where alcohol is legally available. From a purely economic PoV, their impact
is considerable as a knock-on effect on the hospitality sector, even as their effect on the liquor
industry itself is reduced by consumers stocking up in advance. This shows up in states where
tourism is a significant contributor. Business dislocation is compounded by potential artificial
scarcity and bootlegging. Dry days usually fly under the radar of economic impact assessment
as opposed to outright prohibition because the effects are temporary. Yet, the two measures

IV. No more Mr Nice Guy. Five years after the Covid pandemic forced employers to embrace
empathy and flexibility, bosses are back to laying down the law. Tough talk is everywhere:
JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon blasted remote workers for being hard to reach on Fridays while
Google co-founder Sergey Brin insisted in a memo that “60 hours a week is the sweet spot of
productivity”.

The shift goes beyond talk. The shifting balance of power between companies and their
workers has multiple roots. The political context certainly favours bosses: US President Donald
Trump has publicly questioned the value of the federal work force, let go thousands of
government employees and ended collective bargaining for 1mn more. He is also reshaping the
National Labor Relations Board, which enforces worker-protection rules, by firing its chair and
adding two members that unions describe as “anti-worker”. The economic backdrop has also
strengthened management’s hand. While US unemployment remains relatively low, many
workers who do not like their jobs cannot readily find alternatives. US-based companies have
announced more than 800,000 job cuts so far this year, the most since the height of the
pandemic. Companies have been further empowered by the rapid rise of large language models
and other artificial intelligence. Many employers are holding off on hiring new workers while
they wait to see whether AI can make their existing workforce more productive — or replace
labour entirely.

Still there are limits to the amount of control that employers can exercise over their employees.
Employees have countered the demands for an always-on, ever-present workforce with a series
of subversive strategies. Social media is full of terms such as “coffee badging”, slang for
showing up to the office just long enough to swipe in and grab a cuppa, and “quiet vacationing”
— scheduling emails and setting up automatic responses to disguise time away. Strict rules,
demands for long hours and lay-off threats may boost corporate bottom lines initially, but there
are big risks to this strategy. AI is great for routine tasks, processing data and simple coding.
But more complex work will still require humans for the foreseeable future, and people with


top skills remain in high demand. On the flip side, bosses who bang on about how loyalty is
passé should not be surprised when their top people start to act like star athletes and offer
themselves to the highest bidder. If you are still counting on humans to handle your company’s
most complicated and high-stakes decisions, it seems like a poor strategy to alienate them
ahead of time.

V. Large and intensely black; thick, velvety fur; has a faint fringe of white hair across his chest;
not easy to find in ordinary light.” When his daughter Clara’s beloved black cat Bambino
disappeared while she was convalescing in a sanatorium, Mark Twain put out the ad in the
New York American and spent days receiving strangers with abandoned black cats in the hope
of finding Bambino among them. The cat returned on his own, but it was no secret in New York
that the American writer loved his daughter, and Bambino, with equal fervour.

That they occupy a special place in the lives of their humans is no secret. But separated by
centuries and continents, the spurt in litigation and mediations in India’s capital over pets and
strays only goes to show that the law is just beginning to catch up with what the heart has
always known: That animals matter — not as assets, but as companions. And, in some
circumstances, they are the bone of contention or caught between adversaries. Take, for
instance, a civil suit filed in 2023 by an advocate against his neighbours in south Delhi. The
reason: Their pet had chased him, leading him to fall and fracture his wrists. When TMC MP
Mahua Moitra broke up with lawyer Jai Anant Dehadrai, the bitterness spilled over into a
custody tussle over their beloved Rottweiler, Henry.

It may seem trivial to some, absurd even, but these disputes, at their core, are declarations of
how much trust is conveyed through a wag of a tail or the flick of a feline ear. In lonely, crowded
urban metropolises, pets provide the kind of unstinting comfort that few can. Neighbours fight,
lovers part, but what lingers is the bond with the creature left in between. Reforms to Australian
law last month recognised this: For the first time, in cases of separation, Australian courts will
factor in emotional attachment when determining pet ownership. As Delhi courts navigate this
tricky terrain, it is a reminder that love, no matter how small or furry, always leaves a trail.

neutrality, stability, and institutional dignity. Motions seeking the removal of a Presiding
Officer are exceptional mechanisms embedded within constitutional and procedural
frameworks to balance accountability with independence. Such motions are governed by strict
notice requirements and voting procedures, reflecting the importance of shielding the Chair

custodian of House rules, order, and legislative continuity. Legal scholars note that challenges
to the Speaker’s position often raise broader issues of constitutional morality, federal politics,
and legislative ethics. These episodes also highlight the tension between partisan mobilisation
and the institutional safeguards necessary for democratic functioning. As legislatures face
increasingly adversarial politics, procedural rigor remains central to maintaining public trust

proceedings often reignites debate about transparency, privacy, and due process. In recent
years, disclosures connected to long-running investigations into abuse and trafficking networks
have drawn global attention, particularly where sealed records, depositions, and evidentiary
filings are concerned. Legal experts emphasise that such releases typically occur under judicial


supervision and are governed by procedural rules balancing public interest with the rights of
individuals not convicted of crimes. In the United States, unsealed records may include names,
testimonies, or correspondence, but do not automatically imply guilt. The episode has renewed
scrutiny of how courts handle sensitive evidence, the role of investigative journalism, and the
ethical limits of public disclosure. It also highlights the enduring tension between
accountability in powerful circles and foundational legal principles such as presumption of
innocence.

Source: The Guardian

diplomatic backdrop, where cricket functions as both a competitive spectacle and a symbolic
arena of engagement. The lead-up to the T20 World Cup 2026 has again drawn attention to

X. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a bailment creates a relationship of trust and specific
reciprocal obligations. While the bailee’s duty of care is paramount, the law concomitantly
imposes several critical duties on the bailor to ensure fairness and facilitate the purpose of the
bailment. Primarily, the bailor has a duty to disclose faults in the goods bailed, a obligation
detailed in Section 150. This duty varies significantly based on the nature of the bailment. In
a gratuitous bailment (for the sole benefit of the bailee), the bailor is bound to disclose only
known faults that could expose the bailee to an “extraordinary risk.” Conversely, in a non-
gratuitous or reward-based bailment, the standard is stricter; the bailor is liable for any defect,
whether known or unknown, which materially interferes with the intended use of the goods,
effectively implying a warranty of fitness.

Furthermore, the bailor bears financial responsibilities. As per Section 158, in a gratuitous
bailment, the bailor must repay the bailee all necessary expenses incurred for preserving or
protecting the bailed goods. This ensures the bailee is not out of pocket for acting in the
bailor’s interest. A more profound duty arises from the bailor’s title to the goods. Section 164
stipulates that if the bailor has no valid title to the goods and the bailee consequently suffers a
loss—such as being compelled to deliver the goods to the true owner—the bailor is under a
duty to indemnify the bailee for such loss. This protects an innocent bailee from the
consequences of the bailor’s defective ownership.

Finally, the bailment relationship concludes with the duty to receive back the goods upon the
fulfilment of its purpose or the expiry of its term, as implied under Section 164. A refusal to
accept the returned goods would unjustly extend the bailee’s liability and possession. Thus,


the bailor’s duties—ranging from disclosure and indemnity to acceptance—form an essential
framework that supports the bailee’s performance and upholds the equitable foundations of
the contract of bailment.

       does not inform Bela. During the trip, the front brake fails on a steep hill, causing an
       accident and significant damage to the motorcycle. Bela seeks compensation from
       Amit for the repair costs. Is Amit liable?
options:
The liability should be apportioned between both parties since Bela also assumed
           some risk by using an old vehicle.

Amit is not liable for the damages because the bailment was entirely for Bela's
           benefit with no payment involved.

Amit is liable because he failed to disclose a known fault posing an extraordinary
           risk in a gratuitous bailment.

Amit would only be held liable if Bela could successfully prove in court that Amit
           had prior knowledge of the specific mechanical fault.

content.passageText:
XI. In a significant jurisprudential shift, a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court has recalled
its own 2025 Vanashakti judgment, which had imposed an absolute prohibition on ex post facto
or retrospective Environmental Clearances (ECs). This ruling acknowledges the complex
tension between uncompromising environmental protection and pragmatic developmental
imperatives.

Ex post facto ECs refer to approvals granted after a project has commenced operations or
construction without the mandated prior clearance, effectively regularizing a violation. The
Vanashakti judgment had correctly identified these as an "anathema" to core environmental
principles, notably the precautionary principle enshrined in the Environment (Protection) Act,
1986, and EIA Notifications, which mandate prior assessment to prevent harm. It struck down
government instruments permitting such regularisation as a "gross illegality."

However, the recalling bench, in a 2:1 decision, held that the absolute ban was per incuriam—
rendered without due care for binding precedents. It highlighted that coordinate benches in


Alembic Pharmaceuticals (2020) and D. Swamy (2021) had, while discouraging the practice,
allowed regularization in exceptional circumstances with stringent penalties. The Court
invoked the principle of proportionality, reasoning that the remedy of demolition for procedural
lapses—where projects, often involving substantial public investment, began without EC due
to administrative delays rather than malafide intent—could cause disproportionate public harm.
It emphasized that the objective of environmental compliance could be achieved through heavy
monetary penalties and compulsory restoration measures, thereby bringing errant projects
under a regulatory umbrella without necessitating their wasteful destruction.

Consequently, the Court has referred the issue to a larger bench for authoritative reconciliation.
This move underscores a judicial attempt to balance ecological integrity with developmental
reality. It implicitly mandates that any future framework for exceptional ex post facto
regularisation must be coupled with robust deterrent penalties, rigorous monitoring via tools
like PARIVESH, and enforceable restoration obligations under the Polluter Pays Principle,
ensuring that expediency does not eclipse accountability.

Principle of Non-Retrogression

content.passageText:
XI. In a significant jurisprudential shift, a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court has recalled
its own 2025 Vanashakti judgment, which had imposed an absolute prohibition on ex post facto
or retrospective Environmental Clearances (ECs). This ruling acknowledges the complex
tension between uncompromising environmental protection and pragmatic developmental
imperatives.

Ex post facto ECs refer to approvals granted after a project has commenced operations or
construction without the mandated prior clearance, effectively regularizing a violation. The
Vanashakti judgment had correctly identified these as an "anathema" to core environmental
principles, notably the precautionary principle enshrined in the Environment (Protection) Act,
1986, and EIA Notifications, which mandate prior assessment to prevent harm. It struck down
government instruments permitting such regularisation as a "gross illegality."

However, the recalling bench, in a 2:1 decision, held that the absolute ban was per incuriam—
rendered without due care for binding precedents. It highlighted that coordinate benches in


Alembic Pharmaceuticals (2020) and D. Swamy (2021) had, while discouraging the practice,
allowed regularization in exceptional circumstances with stringent penalties. The Court
invoked the principle of proportionality, reasoning that the remedy of demolition for procedural
lapses—where projects, often involving substantial public investment, began without EC due
to administrative delays rather than malafide intent—could cause disproportionate public harm.
It emphasized that the objective of environmental compliance could be achieved through heavy
monetary penalties and compulsory restoration measures, thereby bringing errant projects
under a regulatory umbrella without necessitating their wasteful destruction.

Consequently, the Court has referred the issue to a larger bench for authoritative reconciliation.
This move underscores a judicial attempt to balance ecological integrity with developmental
reality. It implicitly mandates that any future framework for exceptional ex post facto
regularisation must be coupled with robust deterrent penalties, rigorous monitoring via tools
like PARIVESH, and enforceable restoration obligations under the Polluter Pays Principle,
ensuring that expediency does not eclipse accountability.

content.passageText:
XII. The Indian Penal Code, 1860, meticulously defines offences but also incorporates
essential General Defences (Sections 76-106) that absolve or mitigate liability by negating the
requisite mens rea or justifying the act. These defences are fundamental to a just criminal
jurisprudence, recognizing that not every harmful act constitutes a crime. A key defence is
Mistake of Fact, where a person acting under a genuine and reasonable mistaken belief of fact
is excused, as it negatives criminal intention. Similarly, acts performed by judges or officers
pursuant to Judicial and Executive Acts are protected when done in good faith under court
orders or legal authority.

The IPC excuses harm caused by an Accident (Sec. 80)—a purely unfortunate event occurring
despite ordinary care and without criminal intent. Conversely, the defence of Necessity (Sec.
81) justifies an act done to prevent greater harm, provided the act was necessary and the harm
caused was proportionate. The law also prescribes exemptions based on capacity. Infancy
completely exempts a child below seven and conditionally those between seven and twelve, if
lacking maturity of understanding. Insanity (Sec. 84) is a complete defence, adhering to the
M’Naghten Rules, requiring proof that the accused, due to unsoundness of mind, was incapable
of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong.

Intoxication (Sec. 85-86) provides a nuanced defence. Involuntary intoxication can excuse if it
renders the person incapable of forming intent. However, voluntary intoxication is generally
no defence, except potentially for proving the absence of a specific intent in certain crimes. A
vital justificatory defence is the Right of Private Defence (Sec. 96-106), which empowers
individuals to protect their own or another’s body and property against imminent unlawful
aggression, subject to the cardinal principle of proportionality. Furthermore, Consent can be a
defence, but only if it is free, informed, and given by a competent person, and never for acts
intended or known to cause grievous hurt or death. Finally, the law disregards Trivial Acts (Sec.
95) causing harm so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain.


Collectively, these defences ensure the penal code punishes only blameworthy conduct,
balancing societal protection with individual justice.

content.passageText:
XIII. The law of torts provides justifications or defences which, when successfully pleaded,
can absolve or mitigate a defendant’s liability, balancing the plaintiff’s right to compensation
against equitable exceptions. A foundational defence is Volenti Non Fit Injuria, which asserts
that one who voluntarily and knowingly assumes a risk cannot subsequently complain of the
harm. This applies to clear scenarios like participating in a contact sport, but courts scrutinise
the voluntariness and adequacy of consent, especially in employer-employee relationships.

Closely related is Contributory Negligence, where the plaintiff’s own failure to take reasonable
care for their safety contributes to the damage. Historically, this was a complete bar to recovery.
However, in India, through judicial evolution and statutory amendments like the Motor
Vehicles Act, courts now apportion liability using the principle of comparative negligence,
awarding damages reduced by the plaintiff’s share of fault.

Certain events negate human agency altogether. An Act of God (vis major) refers to an
overwhelming natural cause without human intervention, like an unprecedented flood, while
Inevitable Accident denotes an unexpected event despite all reasonable precautions. Both
defences succeed by proving the harm was unforeseeable and unavoidable. Justificatory
defences include the Right of Private Defence, permitting reasonable force to protect one’s


person or property from imminent threat, and Necessity, which excuses an act causing lesser
harm to prevent a greater, imminent danger—key distinctions being the source of the threat
and the absence of fault in necessity.

A complete defence is Statutory Authority, where the act complained of is expressly permitted
by law. Conversely, Mistake, whether of fact or law, is generally not a defence in tort, as
liability often hinges on the act itself, not the defendant’s subjective intent. Finally, the
procedural defence of Limitation is critical; a suit must be filed within the prescribed period
(typically one to three years from the date the wrong is discovered). Failure to do so
extinguishes the remedy, regardless of the merit of the claim, underscoring the law’s interest in
finality and diligence.

XIII. The law of torts provides justifications or defences which, when successfully pleaded,
can absolve or mitigate a defendant’s liability, balancing the plaintiff’s right to compensation
against equitable exceptions. A foundational defence is Volenti Non Fit Injuria, which asserts
that one who voluntarily and knowingly assumes a risk cannot subsequently complain of the
harm. This applies to clear scenarios like participating in a contact sport, but courts scrutinise
the voluntariness and adequacy of consent, especially in employer-employee relationships.

Closely related is Contributory Negligence, where the plaintiff’s own failure to take reasonable
care for their safety contributes to the damage. Historically, this was a complete bar to recovery.
However, in India, through judicial evolution and statutory amendments like the Motor
Vehicles Act, courts now apportion liability using the principle of comparative negligence,
awarding damages reduced by the plaintiff’s share of fault.

Certain events negate human agency altogether. An Act of God (vis major) refers to an
overwhelming natural cause without human intervention, like an unprecedented flood, while
Inevitable Accident denotes an unexpected event despite all reasonable precautions. Both
defences succeed by proving the harm was unforeseeable and unavoidable. Justificatory
defences include the Right of Private Defence, permitting reasonable force to protect one’s


person or property from imminent threat, and Necessity, which excuses an act causing lesser
harm to prevent a greater, imminent danger—key distinctions being the source of the threat
and the absence of fault in necessity.

A complete defence is Statutory Authority, where the act complained of is expressly permitted
by law. Conversely, Mistake, whether of fact or law, is generally not a defence in tort, as
liability often hinges on the act itself, not the defendant’s subjective intent. Finally, the
procedural defence of Limitation is critical; a suit must be filed within the prescribed period
(typically one to three years from the date the wrong is discovered). Failure to do so
extinguishes the remedy, regardless of the merit of the claim, underscoring the law’s interest in
finality and diligence.

XIV. The recent India Justice Report starkly exposes the systemic failures impeding India’s
juvenile justice framework, revealing a profound gap between the rehabilitative ideals of the
Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 and its implementation. The most
critical failure is the high pendency of cases, with over 55% of matters before Juvenile Justice
Boards (JJBs) pending, directly contradicting the Act’s mandate for speedy, child-centric
inquiry. This delay is exacerbated by structural gaps in JJB constitution, where 24% of boards
lack full membership, undermining quorum and informed decision-making. Compounding this
is the absence of legal services clinics in 30% of JJBs, violating children's right to timely legal
aid and fair procedure.

These operational deficiencies are rooted in deeper systemic administrative weaknesses,
including poor inter-agency coordination and a stark lack of transparency, evidenced by weak
RTI compliance. The absence of a unified National Data Grid fragments oversight, preventing
effective monitoring across police, child protection services, and legal authorities. While the
2015 Act marked a progressive shift by establishing JJBs for rehabilitation and empowering
CARA for adoption, its potential is neutralized by these bottlenecks. The 2021 Amendment,
which made certain offences non-cognisable and empowered District Magistrates in adoption,
addresses symptoms but not the core infrastructural crisis.

Consequently, urgent reform measures are imperative. Strengthening institutional
infrastructure by ensuring fully staffed JJBs with attached legal clinics is foundational. The
focus must pivot decisively from custodial approaches to robust rehabilitation and reintegration


within Child Care Institutions (CCIs), supported by vocational and psychological services.
Ultimately, creating a centralized public data portal is essential for tracking pendency,
monitoring child welfare, and enforcing accountability. Without these interventions, the
legislative promise of a justice system that prioritizes the child’s best interest and dignity
remains unfulfilled, perpetuating procedural injustice over protection.

content.passageText:
XV. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956, is the definitive statute governing intestate succession
for Hindus, including Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs. It establishes a uniform and secular code,
replacing the traditional textual law of the Mitakshara and Dayabhaga schools. Its primary
objective is to systematize the rules of inheritance, bringing clarity and gender justice to the
devolution of property.

The Act's applicability extends to any person who is a Hindu by religion, in any form, including
Virashaivas and Lingayats, and to those belonging to the religions mentioned. A core feature
of the Act is the creation of a statutory hierarchy of heirs, supplanting the traditional sapinda
and gotraja systems. This hierarchy is structured into four tiers: Class I heirs, Class II heirs
(listed in an order of precedence), Agnates, and Cognates. Class I heirs, such as the widow,
mother, son, daughter, and descendants of pre-deceased children, take precedence
simultaneously, excluding all others. Only in their absence do subsequent categories inherit.

Central to the Act's operation is the concept of the coparcenary, a distinct entity within a Joint
Hindu Family comprising a common ancestor and his lineal male descendants within three
generations. The revolutionary 2005 Amendment accorded the daughter the status of a
coparcener by birth, granting her rights and liabilities equal to a son. Coparcenary property
refers to ancestral property in which each coparcener holds an undivided, birthright interest.
This contrasts with separate or self-acquired property, which an individual procures through
personal effort, free from ancestral lineage.

Upon the death of a coparcener, the mechanism of notional partition is invoked. This legal
fiction deems a partition of the coparcenary to have occurred immediately before the member's
death, crystallizing his share. This ascertained share then devolves not by survivorship to the
remaining coparceners, but by testamentary disposition or, in its absence, via intestate
succession under the Act to his own legal heirs. This intricate interplay between the law of
coparcenary and the statutory scheme of heirs ensures a structured and equitable distribution
of a Hindu's estate.

content.passageText:
XIX. Creative writing used to be a human prerogative: do it well, do it badly, but either way
endorse the consensus that to write about human experience was worth the candle and the
coffee. Here was an essential human act, so much so that poetry formed a critical part of the
computer pioneer Alan Turing’s original test: to determine whether an unseen respondent to a
series of questions was human or a mechanical imposter. The Turing Test is often simplified to
denote a single crossing point between two territories, human and machine. Pass the test, and
artificial intelligence can stroll on over to our side of the line. Take a look around. Decide what
to do with us. But, first, it has to pass.

In the paper ‘Computing Machinery and Intelligence’ (1950), published in the journal Mind,
Turing set out his objective: ‘to consider the question, “Can machines think?”’ In true human
fashion, he immediately re-phrases the question, at some length, and eventually arrives at the
‘imitation game’, modelled on a drawing-room entertainment from before the internet, before
television. The original game he has in mind involves a guesser in the hotseat who poses
questions to a man (X) and a woman (Y), who are out of sight and hearing in a separate room.
The guesser has to determine from their written answers which is the man and which is the
woman. X tries to mislead, and wins if the guesser is wrong; Y wins if the guesser is right. Try
it, it’s fun.

In this context, the first question posed in Turing’s proposed test is less surprising than at first
it seems: ‘Will X please tell me the length of his or her hair?’ Next, Turing asks, equally
politely: ‘Please write me a sonnet on the subject of the Forth Bridge.’ Two questions in, and
the contested boundary between human and machine thinking is already looking for answers
in literature, in art. Turing’s 1950s version of X – the participant aiming to mislead – replies:
‘Count me out on this one. I never could write poetry.’ To imagine this answer, in the second
phase of his game, Turing’s complicated brain is playing the role of a machine playing X,


hidden from sight and typing its answers, pretending to be a man (who previously played the
game pretending to be a woman). I know, but if the test were easy an air-fryer could pass it.

[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Computers can’t surprise”, aeon.]

content.passageText:
XIX. Creative writing used to be a human prerogative: do it well, do it badly, but either way
endorse the consensus that to write about human experience was worth the candle and the
coffee. Here was an essential human act, so much so that poetry formed a critical part of the
computer pioneer Alan Turing’s original test: to determine whether an unseen respondent to a
series of questions was human or a mechanical imposter. The Turing Test is often simplified to
denote a single crossing point between two territories, human and machine. Pass the test, and
artificial intelligence can stroll on over to our side of the line. Take a look around. Decide what
to do with us. But, first, it has to pass.

In the paper ‘Computing Machinery and Intelligence’ (1950), published in the journal Mind,
Turing set out his objective: ‘to consider the question, “Can machines think?”’ In true human
fashion, he immediately re-phrases the question, at some length, and eventually arrives at the
‘imitation game’, modelled on a drawing-room entertainment from before the internet, before
television. The original game he has in mind involves a guesser in the hotseat who poses
questions to a man (X) and a woman (Y), who are out of sight and hearing in a separate room.
The guesser has to determine from their written answers which is the man and which is the
woman. X tries to mislead, and wins if the guesser is wrong; Y wins if the guesser is right. Try
it, it’s fun.

In this context, the first question posed in Turing’s proposed test is less surprising than at first
it seems: ‘Will X please tell me the length of his or her hair?’ Next, Turing asks, equally
politely: ‘Please write me a sonnet on the subject of the Forth Bridge.’ Two questions in, and
the contested boundary between human and machine thinking is already looking for answers
in literature, in art. Turing’s 1950s version of X – the participant aiming to mislead – replies:
‘Count me out on this one. I never could write poetry.’ To imagine this answer, in the second
phase of his game, Turing’s complicated brain is playing the role of a machine playing X,


hidden from sight and typing its answers, pretending to be a man (who previously played the
game pretending to be a woman). I know, but if the test were easy an air-fryer could pass it.

[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Computers can’t surprise”, aeon.]

content.passageText:
I. Logitech CEO Hanneke Faber has set the AI cat among boardroom pigeons. She says she'd
welcome a bot member in every board meeting to stay ahead in the productivity curve. AI
agents are embedding themselves across business functions, and it is a matter of time before
they show up on company boards with their unbeatable data-driven analytical capabilities.
Bots have access to real-time business processes on a scale impossible to reach by humans.
Board decisions made on inputs by AI agents will be vastly superior, as will their execution
through digital agents. Faber is correct. Bring AI on board - but do it with circumspection.
Boardrooms exist not only to maximise corporate profits but also to ensure they are made
ethically. Corporate governance will have to remain entirely in the domain of humans given
AI's shortcomings. Culture and emotions drive corporate growth alongside business strategy.
The middle ground would be for boardrooms to power themselves up through AI bots and
then turn the decision-making over to directors for the human touch. Conflict resolution
between digital and human inputs would necessarily have to be guided by value judgement.
Boardrooms by design are good at asking ethical questions. They would get better at it if the
questions became granular through the introduction of AI-driven business strategies.
Corporate boards that use augmented intelligence are likely to improve productivity without
losing agency over governance. The composition of future boardrooms will be vital to
achieving the right balance between artificial and natural intelligence. Boards guide corporate
engagement with the external environment, and the pace of incorporating AI-driven decisions
will be influenced by technology dispersal. Business, however, is expected to push societal
adoption of AI and will have to work out the place for bots in decision-making. Humans will
have to be in the loop at almost every stage of AI implementation to be able to retain context
for intervention. Behind every R2D2, there must be a Luke Skywalker.

ai-incorporated/articleshow/124641380.cms?from=mdr

II. Stodgy textbooks tell you that collective bargaining began with the industrial revolution
and workers seeking to protect themselves against exploitation. You have updated the concept
as more jobs now come from outside factories, mills and mines. But it’s still associated with
the grim fight for minimum pay, accident insurance, transparency in algorithms…So you
might be shook that JITO, an Ahmedabad-based group of Jain industrialists, businessmen and
professionals, has used collective bargaining to get themselves Audis, BMWs, Mercs…They
jiffed top luxury brands into giving them a Rs 21cr discount.
Actually, the Richie Rich are not new to this romp at all. Different Indian mercantile
communities historically grew by negotiating with the colonialists as a coordinated bloc. In
the West, families like the Rothschilds and Agnellis grew into their extraordinary wealth and
power through mobilising oversized leverage. Family controlled conglomerates from Japan’s
Mitsubishi and Mitsui to South Korea’s Samsung and LG have done the same to get
favourable industrial policies and trade protections. BTW, what do you think oil barons of
Opec do? The Silicon Valley bros may compete aggressively with each other but they also
often act collectively, as when lobbying against proposed antitrust or privacy laws. So, if in
your head, it’s workers, wage earners, gig hands alone who are acting as a class, maybe have
a rethink.
If we book a bunch of hotel rooms for a family function, we demand a discount. If the real
moneybags buy some prime real estate in London or Mumbai, they do the same. Same
difference. The Rolex, Hermès and Ferraris also line up to do the tiptop for them. Jets, yachts,
vineyards, yes, they negotiate great prices for all these. Because they can. Not everyone
tattles like JITO though. Most golden bargains stay behind gilded curtains.
SOURCE: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-editorials/luxediscount/

III. Days after brokering a fragile ceasefire in West Asia, US President Donald Trump has
turned his attention once again to Eastern Europe. His stance on the ongoing three-and-a-half-
year war has swung like a pendulum. In February, the Oval Office spat with Ukrainian
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was followed by threats of sanctions against Moscow. Then
at the Alaska Summit in August, Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin and appeared
to align himself with the Kremlin’s position — particularly Putin’s demand that Ukraine cede
unoccupied parts of the Donbas region in exchange for a ceasefire. Subsequently, Trump
threw his weight behind Kyiv and speculated in September that Ukraine could take back all
of its territory and “maybe even go further than that”. He even expressed openness to the idea
of supplying Tomahawk cruise missiles to Ukraine. Now, there is yet another reversal.
Following a lengthy call with Putin last week and a meeting with Zelenskyy on Friday,
Trump has urged Kyiv and Moscow to “stop where they are”, suggested that the war should
end by allowing the Donbas region to “be cut the way it is” (leaving most of it under Russian
control), and rejected Zelenskyy’s request for the Tomahawks.


Trump’s inconsistency is all too familiar and yet disquieting, not just for Ukraine, but also for
Europe. Over the past six weeks, Russia has sent drones over Poland and Romania, flown
fighter jets into Estonian airspace, and is accused of orchestrating drone flights that disrupted
airports in Denmark, Belgium, and Germany — allegations Moscow has denied. At the time,
Trump expressed clear solidarity with NATO, declaring that it should shoot down Russian
aircraft violating its airspace. Now, as the US president again presses Ukraine to make
concessions, it will be up to Europe to ensure that, in the event of a deal, robust security
assurances are provided to Ukraine.
An erratic Trump and an emboldened Putin illustrate the challenges that lie ahead in ending
the war. Trump has reportedly agreed to hold another summit in Hungary — an EU member
that opposes Ukraine’s accession and is led by the pro-Putin Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
Once again, it appears that Ukraine and Europe are being sidelined, with Washington
positioning itself as the arbiter of war and peace. If this trend continues, and given the US
president’s current stance, the day may not be far when Ukraine is left with little choice but to
yield to Trump’s terms and compromise on its territory. To avert that scenario, Europe will
need to act quickly.
SOURCE:https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/editorials/erratic-trump-and-emboldened-
putin-why-ending-ukraine-war-is-so-complex-10319716/

year war has swung like a pendulum. In February, the Oval Office spat with Ukrainian
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was followed by threats of sanctions against Moscow. Then
at the Alaska Summit in August, Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin and appeared
to align himself with the Kremlin’s position — particularly Putin’s demand that Ukraine cede
unoccupied parts of the Donbas region in exchange for a ceasefire. Subsequently, Trump
threw his weight behind Kyiv and speculated in September that Ukraine could take back all
of its territory and “maybe even go further than that”. He even expressed openness to the idea
of supplying Tomahawk cruise missiles to Ukraine. Now, there is yet another reversal.
Following a lengthy call with Putin last week and a meeting with Zelenskyy on Friday,
Trump has urged Kyiv and Moscow to “stop where they are”, suggested that the war should
end by allowing the Donbas region to “be cut the way it is” (leaving most of it under Russian
control), and rejected Zelenskyy’s request for the Tomahawks.


Trump’s inconsistency is all too familiar and yet disquieting, not just for Ukraine, but also for
Europe. Over the past six weeks, Russia has sent drones over Poland and Romania, flown
fighter jets into Estonian airspace, and is accused of orchestrating drone flights that disrupted
airports in Denmark, Belgium, and Germany — allegations Moscow has denied. At the time,
Trump expressed clear solidarity with NATO, declaring that it should shoot down Russian
aircraft violating its airspace. Now, as the US president again presses Ukraine to make
concessions, it will be up to Europe to ensure that, in the event of a deal, robust security
assurances are provided to Ukraine.
An erratic Trump and an emboldened Putin illustrate the challenges that lie ahead in ending
the war. Trump has reportedly agreed to hold another summit in Hungary — an EU member
that opposes Ukraine’s accession and is led by the pro-Putin Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
Once again, it appears that Ukraine and Europe are being sidelined, with Washington
positioning itself as the arbiter of war and peace. If this trend continues, and given the US
president’s current stance, the day may not be far when Ukraine is left with little choice but to
yield to Trump’s terms and compromise on its territory. To avert that scenario, Europe will
need to act quickly.

content.passageText:
IV. India is quietly approaching a demographic turning point that its political vocabulary has
yet to fully acknowledge. While public debate remains dominated by growth rates,
employment numbers, and infrastructure expansion, a far slower transformation is unfolding
beneath the surface ~ the steady ageing of the population, often in isolation and uncertainty.
For decades, Indian society relied on the family as the primary institution of elder care. That
assumption is now fraying. Urban migration, smaller households, longer life expectancy, and
changing social norms have altered how ageing is experienced.
A growing number of older Indians are living alone or with equally frail spouses, navigating
declining health with limited daily support. What was once absorbed privately within
households is increasingly becoming a public challenge. The consequences are not merely
emotional. Ageing brings predictable medical and functional needs ~ mobility assistance,
chronic disease management, memory care, and companionship. Yet India’s health system
remains overwhelmingly designed for acute treatment rather than long-term care. Hospitals
may address illness, but they are poorly equipped to support ageing. Policy responses exist,
but they operate in silos.


Private assisted living facilities and specialised care homes are expanding, but they remain
out of reach for most Indians. Meanwhile, publicly supported elder-care institutions are too
few to meet even a fraction of the demand. The result is an uncomfortable gap between
longevity and dignity. There is also a deeper societal cost. Loneliness among older adults is
no longer an exception. Social isolation contributes to mental distress, accelerates physical
decline, and increases dependence on emergency healthcare. These outcomes ultimately place
greater strain on public systems ~ the very systems that proactive investment could
strengthen rather than overwhelm. India’s ageing challenge should therefore be viewed not as
a welfare obligation alone, but as a matter of long-term economic planning. Countries that
age without preparing for care infrastructure often pay later through rising healthcare costs,
reduced workforce participation among caregivers, and widening inequality between those
who can afford support and those who cannot. What is needed is a shift in thinking.
SOURCE: https://www.thestatesman.com/opinion/ageing-alone-1503549132.html

V. Union Home Minister Amit Shah has rightly stressed the need to make a distinction between
refugees and infiltrators. Although valid, the problem lies in the application of objective
parameters by those in power to draw distinctions. Even where proper policy and a legal
framework exist, issues may arise. Also at play is the level of official understanding. In India,
which is not a signatory to the 1951 UN Refugee Convention and the 1967 Protocol, there is
no comprehensive single law defining who a refugee is, leaving scope for arbitrary action. Till
the end of March 2025, apart from the Citizenship Act 1955 and the Passports Act 1967, three
laws (the Foreigners Act, 1946, the Registration of Foreigners Act, 1939 and the Passport
(Entry into India) Act, 1920) were applied to deal with foreign nationals, including refuge
seekers. From April, the Immigration and Foreigners Act replaced the three pre-Independence
laws and subsumed the Immigration (Carriers’ Liability) Act, 2000. While this streamlined the
legal framework, the absence of a refugee policy document has also led to different yardsticks
for the refugee community in India. While there was a rehabilitation policy in 2014 for about
63,000 Tibetan refugees, there is no such document for the nearly 90,000 Sri Lankan Tamils.
At the end of June 2023, the population of refugees or persons of concern in India was over
2.11 lakh (also counting those from Myanmar, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Africa and West Asia).
Any undocumented or overstaying refugee is regarded as an illegal migrant (Citizenship Act).
He can also be called an infiltrator. Thus, genuine and harmless refugees risk facing
harassment.
Even though the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 was aimed at providing citizenship to six
religious minorities belonging to Bangladesh, Pakistan and Afghanistan, it drew sharp criticism
as it discriminated on the lines of religion and left out sections of Muslims, and also Sri Lankan


Tamils and the Rohingya, both minorities in their countries. But in a notification last month,
undocumented or overstaying Tamil refugees, who have registered themselves with the
authorities, were granted exemption from penal provisions of the Immigration and Foreigners
Act, provided they took shelter in India on or before January 9, 2015. Other groups, too have
been covered. Still, there is no change in the recent trend of religion-based exclusions. There
is nothing fundamentally wrong with the approach of discreet humanitarian relief to refugees
in general but this has to be backed by consistent, rational and fair treatment for all.


SOURCE:https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/editorial/refugees-and-infiltrators-on-different-
yardsticks-for-indias-refugee-community/article70167639.ece

laws (the Foreigners Act, 1946, the Registration of Foreigners Act, 1939 and the Passport
(Entry into India) Act, 1920) were applied to deal with foreign nationals, including refuge
seekers. From April, the Immigration and Foreigners Act replaced the three pre-Independence
laws and subsumed the Immigration (Carriers’ Liability) Act, 2000. While this streamlined the
legal framework, the absence of a refugee policy document has also led to different yardsticks
for the refugee community in India. While there was a rehabilitation policy in 2014 for about
63,000 Tibetan refugees, there is no such document for the nearly 90,000 Sri Lankan Tamils.
At the end of June 2023, the population of refugees or persons of concern in India was over
2.11 lakh (also counting those from Myanmar, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Africa and West Asia).
Any undocumented or overstaying refugee is regarded as an illegal migrant (Citizenship Act).
He can also be called an infiltrator. Thus, genuine and harmless refugees risk facing
harassment.
Even though the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 was aimed at providing citizenship to six
religious minorities belonging to Bangladesh, Pakistan and Afghanistan, it drew sharp criticism
as it discriminated on the lines of religion and left out sections of Muslims, and also Sri Lankan


Tamils and the Rohingya, both minorities in their countries. But in a notification last month,
undocumented or overstaying Tamil refugees, who have registered themselves with the
authorities, were granted exemption from penal provisions of the Immigration and Foreigners
Act, provided they took shelter in India on or before January 9, 2015. Other groups, too have
been covered. Still, there is no change in the recent trend of religion-based exclusions. There
is nothing fundamentally wrong with the approach of discreet humanitarian relief to refugees
in general but this has to be backed by consistent, rational and fair treatment for all.

yardsticks-for-indias-refugee-community/article70167639.ece

X. In a landmark judgment reinforcing the constitutional safeguards of judicial independence,
the Supreme Court of India struck down pivotal provisions of the Tribunal Reforms Act, 2021,
declaring them an unconstitutional encroachment by the executive into the judicial domain.
The Court held that the impugned provisions, by granting the Union government excessive
control over appointments, tenure, and service conditions of tribunal members, fundamentally
undermined the autonomy and impartiality of tribunals, thereby violating the separation of
powers—a cornerstone of the Constitution’s basic structure.
The Court meticulously invalidated several stipulations. It ruled the minimum age requirement
of 50 years for appointment as arbitrary, noting it unfairly excluded competent younger
advocates contrary to earlier rulings. The mandated four-year tenure for chairpersons and
members was struck down for fostering dependency and insecurity, with the Court reinstating
a minimum five-year term to ensure institutional continuity. Significantly, the provision


allowing the government a panel of two names per vacancy was nullified, with the directive
that the Search-cum-Selection Committee must recommend only one name to curtail executive
discretion. Equating tribunal members' service conditions with civil servants was also
invalidated, as it blurred the line between judicial and executive functions.
Crucially, the Court condemned the legislative attempt to override its earlier judgment by re-
enacting provisions from a previously invalidated ordinance. It emphatically reiterated that
judicial review is part of the inviolable basic structure, and Parliament cannot nullify a binding
judgment merely by repackaging the same flawed law. To remedy systemic issues, the Court
mandated the establishment of a National Tribunal Commission within four months,
envisioning it as an independent oversight body to ensure transparency and uniformity in
tribunal administration. This decision serves as a potent reaffirmation of constitutional
supremacy, ensuring tribunals—as vital instruments of justice—remain insulated from
executive dominance to uphold fair and specialized adjudication.

content.passageText:
XI. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the creation of a bailment imposes a fiduciary-like
relationship upon the bailee, the party receiving the goods, charging them with several specific
and non-delegable duties central to the arrangement’s integrity. The foremost obligation,
encapsulated in Section 151, is the duty to take reasonable care of the bailed goods. The statute
mandates a uniformly high objective standard: the bailee must exercise the same level of care
as “a man of ordinary prudence” would take of his own goods of similar value and nature. This
standard applies irrespective of whether the bailment is gratuitous or for reward, and failure to
meet it results in liability for any loss, damage, or destruction.
Crucially, the bailee’s right to use the goods is strictly circumscribed by the bailment’s purpose.
Section 154 imposes a duty not to make any unauthorized use of the goods. If the bailee uses
the goods in a manner inconsistent with the terms of the bailment, they become absolutely
liable for any loss or damage occurring during such use, even if caused by an accident or
through no apparent fault. This strict liability underscores the contractual sanctity of the
bailment’s agreed purpose. Furthermore, the bailee has a duty not to mix the bailor’s goods
with their own or a third party’s goods without the bailor’s consent (Sections 155-157).
Unauthorized mixing entitles the bailor to claim compensation for any expenses incurred in
separation or, if the goods cannot be separated, for the resultant loss in value.
Upon the accomplishment of the purpose or the expiry of the stipulated time, the bailee’s duty
under Section 160 is to return, or deliver according to the bailor’s directions, the goods without
waiting for any demand. This duty reinforces the temporary and specific-purpose nature of
bailment. Finally, recognizing the bailor’s enduring ownership, Section 163 obligates the bailee
to return or account for any accretion or benefits that may have accrued from the bailed goods
during the period of bailment, such as offspring from animals or profits earned. Collectively,
these statutory duties position the bailee as a responsible custodian, legally bound to protect


the bailor’s proprietary interest and ensure the goods’ safe return, thereby balancing the benefits
derived from possession with rigorous accountability.

XII. Muslim Succession Law in India remains primarily uncodified, deriving its authoritative
principles from religious texts: the Quran, the traditions of the Prophet (Hadith), and the
interpretative jurisprudence developed by different schools. The two major branches, Sunni
and Shia, have distinct legal frameworks, leading to variations in application while sharing core
concepts. The system is characterized by its mathematical precision and the classification of
heirs into hierarchical categories, balancing fixed divine entitlements with customary tribal
notions of agnatic succession.
The foundational element is the scheme of Fixed Shares (Quranic Heirs/Sharers). Specific
relatives are allotted ordained fractional portions of the estate. Key sharers include the spouse
(1/4 or 1/8), parents (1/6 each), and daughters (1/2 or 2/3 collectively). These shares are
calculated first. The remaining estate, if any, constitutes the residue. This residue devolves to


the Residuaries (Asabat), typically male agnatic relatives like sons, brothers, and uncles, who
inherit per capita after the sharers are satisfied. If no residuary exists, the residue may revert to

XIII. The recent observation by a Supreme Court judge advocating for the decriminalisation of
defamation has reignited a critical constitutional debate in India, centred on the tension between
the fundamental right to reputation and the equally vital right to free speech. Presently,
defamation is governed under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (formerly IPC Sections 499
and 500), which prescribes criminal penalties, including imprisonment. This framework was
constitutionally validated by the Supreme Court in Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India
(2016), which held that protecting reputation is an integral part of the right to life under Article
21 and that criminal defamation constitutes a "reasonable restriction" on free speech under
Article 19(2).
However, growing judicial and academic discourse underscores the pressing need for reform.
Critics argue that criminal defamation is increasingly weaponised by powerful entities,
including political figures and corporations, to silence dissent, settle scores, and stifle
legitimate criticism through the threat of protracted and punitive criminal proceedings. This
creates a significant "chilling effect" on journalists, activists, and citizens, undermining
democratic discourse. Furthermore, the principle of proportionality is questioned, as
reputational harm is primarily a civil injury, and imprisonment is deemed an excessive remedy.
Many mature democracies, notably the United States, treat defamation solely as a civil wrong.
The path forward necessitates a balanced legislative recalibration. A pivotal measure would be
to decriminalise defamation in purely private disputes, restricting criminal liability to
statements concerning public interest that are made with proven actual malice. Concurrently,
civil remedies must be strengthened through fast-track courts, clear norms for compensation,
and promoting alternative dispute resolution to ensure efficient justice. To protect public
watchdogs, statutory safeguards for journalists and whistleblowers acting in good faith, along
with anti-SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation) legislation, are essential to
deter frivolous suits intended to harass. Ultimately, reforming India's defamation law is
imperative to foster a more robust culture of free expression while ensuring that reputation is
protected through civil means that are both effective and constitutionally proportionate.

XIV. The proposal for simultaneous elections, or 'One Nation, One Election,' seeks to realign
the electoral cycles of the Lok Sabha and all State Legislative Assemblies, a practice prevalent
in India’s first two decades. The recent Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024, introduced
following the High-Level Committee (HLC) led by former President Ram Nath Kovind,
provides the legal architecture for this transition. The core legal mechanism involves inserting
Article 82A to empower the Election Commission to synchronize terms and declare a unified
schedule. Crucially, the bill proposes amendments to Articles 83 and 172, stipulating that
assemblies constituted after the foundational "appointed date" would serve only the remainder
of the Lok Sabha’s term, thereby creating a locked cycle for the future.
Proponents, including key governmental committees, argue this reform addresses significant
governance deficits caused by perpetual electioneering. Frequent elections perpetuate policy
paralysis due to the repeated imposition of the Model Code of Conduct, encourage short-term
populist fiscal measures, and place immense logistical strain on administrative and security
resources. Synchronization is posited to ensure political stability, enhance governance
continuity, and allow for more efficient long-term policy implementation by freeing
governments from constant electoral pressure.
However, the initiative faces formidable constitutional and federal challenges. Arbitrarily
curtailing or extending the constitutionally guaranteed five-year term of state assemblies for
mere synchronization raises serious concerns regarding federal autonomy and the basic
structure of the Constitution. It potentially undermines the direct mandate of state electorates
and could disproportionately advantage national parties over regional issues. Furthermore,
logistical hurdles are unprecedented, requiring massive augmentation of EVM/VVPAT
infrastructure and personnel for a single electoral event. The legal framework must also
convincingly address scenarios of premature dissolution through no-confidence motions or
hung houses, ensuring the mechanism does not lead to prolonged instability or presidential
rule.
Therefore, while the pursuit of simultaneous elections aims at enhancing governance
efficiency, its implementation demands rigorous legal scrutiny, broad political consensus, and
robust constitutional safeguards to balance the ideals of administrative convenience with the
foundational principles of democratic federalism and representative accountability.

XV. The doctrine of Absolute Liability is a seminal judicial innovation in Indian tort law,
established by the Supreme Court in the landmark 1987 case of M.C. Mehta vs. Union of India.
This ruling was delivered in the wake of the Oleum gas leak from a Delhi-based unit of Shriram
Food and Fertilizers, an incident that occurred shortly after the catastrophic Bhopal Gas
Tragedy. Recognizing the inadequacy of existing principles, the Court, under Justice Bhagwati,
consciously created a new rule distinct from the English rule of strict liability (Rylands v.
Fletcher). The Court reasoned that the old doctrine, with its numerous exceptions, was
insufficient to address the grave risks posed by modern, profit-driven hazardous industries. The
underlying rationale is that an enterprise which engages in inherently dangerous activity for
economic gain must bear the social responsibility for any harm caused, treating compensation
as a necessary cost of its business operations.
This new principle is critically distinguished from strict liability on two key grounds. First,
while strict liability requires the "escape" of a dangerous thing from the defendant's land,
absolute liability applies even if the harm occurs within the enterprise's premises, such as to
workers or visitors. Second, and most significantly, strict liability admits several exceptions
like Act of God, plaintiff's fault, or act of a third party. Absolute liability admits no exceptions
whatsoever, making the enterprise liable regardless of any supervening circumstance or fault.
As a corollary, the Court integrated the "Polluter Pays" principle, mandating that the offending
enterprise must bear the cost of remediating the damaged environment in addition to
compensating human victims.
In scope and application, the doctrine covers industries like chemical plants, fertilizer units,
nuclear installations, and hazardous waste facilities. The types of harm encompass death,
personal injury, property damage, and environmental degradation. A defining characteristic is
that no traditional defences are admissible; the defendant cannot plead that it took all
reasonable care, that the harm was caused by an Act of God or sabotage, or that the victim was
contributorily negligent. This makes absolute liability the most stringent standard, placing an
unwavering duty of safety on hazardous enterprises.

content.passageText:
XIX. Creative writing used to be a human prerogative: do it well, do it badly, but either way
endorse the consensus that to write about human experience was worth the candle and the
coffee. Here was an essential human act, so much so that poetry formed a critical part of the
computer pioneer Alan Turing’s original test: to determine whether an unseen respondent to a
series of questions was human or a mechanical imposter. The Turing Test is often simplified to
denote a single crossing point between two territories, human and machine. Pass the test, and
artificial intelligence can stroll on over to our side of the line. Take a look around. Decide what
to do with us. But, first, it has to pass.
In the paper ‘Computing Machinery and Intelligence’ (1950), published in the journal Mind,
Turing set out his objective: ‘to consider the question, “Can machines think?”’ In true human
fashion, he immediately re-phrases the question, at some length, and eventually arrives at the
‘imitation game’, modelled on a drawing-room entertainment from before the internet, before
television. The original game he has in mind involves a guesser in the hotseat who poses
questions to a man (X) and a woman (Y), who are out of sight and hearing in a separate room.
The guesser has to determine from their written answers which is the man and which is the
woman. X tries to mislead, and wins if the guesser is wrong; Y wins if the guesser is right. Try
it, it’s fun.
In this context, the first question posed in Turing’s proposed test is less surprising than at first
it seems: ‘Will X please tell me the length of his or her hair?’ Next, Turing asks, equally
politely: ‘Please write me a sonnet on the subject of the Forth Bridge.’ Two questions in, and
the contested boundary between human and machine thinking is already looking for answers
in literature, in art. Turing’s 1950s version of X – the participant aiming to mislead – replies:
‘Count me out on this one. I never could write poetry.’ To imagine this answer, in the second
phase of his game, Turing’s complicated brain is playing the role of a machine playing X,
hidden from sight and typing its answers, pretending to be a man (who previously played the
game pretending to be a woman). I know, but if the test were easy an air-fryer could pass it.


[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Computers can’t surprise”, aeon.]

content.passageText:
I. A new Union Tribal Affairs Ministry policy framework is a reminder that India’s conservation
strategy is not a fortress conservation model but one in which protecting the country’s tigers is
a social contract. The policy’s foremost virtue is reiteration that people living near or inside
forests cannot be relocated until the Forest Rights Act (FRA) 2006 process has been completed,
affirming that they are stakeholders, not trespassers. This view has sadly been falling out of
favour with a government that is increasingly seeing forests solely for their climate utility and
a judiciary keen to settle long-standing disputes. The policy casting relocation as an
“exceptional” measure also overturns the 2024 National Tiger Conservation Authority directive
to remove villages en masse from tiger reserves. Instead of treating humans and tigers as
mutually exclusive, the framework promotes research and pilot projects on sustainable co-
habitation that could help redefine tiger conservation through a more socially legitimate, and
possibly more resilient model. Its invocation of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act for
unlawful evictions and a three-tier system for redress also provide a safety net rarely available
to these communities.

This said, forest-dependent communities have varied needs: some expect hospitals and schools
while others fight to preserve traditional lifestyles. Equally, tigers are sensitive and the reason
many conservationists believe human-free core zones are essential to conserve apex predators.
A national mission to protect tigers on scientific terms needs to ensure such tracts.
Fundamentally, while a national policy protects rights, fine-grained mechanisms sensitive to
particular local conditions are crucial for people and tigers to sustainably coexist. Such
mechanisms are however beyond the ability of top-level Ministries. The conservation
establishment is likely to resist the new policy because it could slow efforts to consolidate tiger
habitats and increase the implementation burden, potentially leading to dual policies on the
ground. In fact, conservation in India is largely controlled by Forest Departments under the
Environment Ministry and States have wide latitude in implementing the FRA. Even in places
where local departments wield significant control, forced relocations may continue in States
that do not enforce the proposed National Framework for Community-Centred Conservation
and Relocation. While existing policy defines compensation criteria and the minimum inviolate
area for a sustainable population, their implementation often violates established principles.
Just as the fortress model has often been insensitive to people’s rights in practice, exiting it
should not mean entering one in which India’s natural riches can be forsworn.

SOURCE:https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/editorial/out-of-the-fortress-on-protecting-
indias-tigers/article70221403.ece

strategy is not a fortress conservation model but one in which protecting the country’s tigers is
a social contract. The policy’s foremost virtue is reiteration that people living near or inside
forests cannot be relocated until the Forest Rights Act (FRA) 2006 process has been completed,
affirming that they are stakeholders, not trespassers. This view has sadly been falling out of
favour with a government that is increasingly seeing forests solely for their climate utility and
a judiciary keen to settle long-standing disputes. The policy casting relocation as an
“exceptional” measure also overturns the 2024 National Tiger Conservation Authority directive
to remove villages en masse from tiger reserves. Instead of treating humans and tigers as
mutually exclusive, the framework promotes research and pilot projects on sustainable co-
habitation that could help redefine tiger conservation through a more socially legitimate, and
possibly more resilient model. Its invocation of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act for
unlawful evictions and a three-tier system for redress also provide a safety net rarely available
to these communities.

This said, forest-dependent communities have varied needs: some expect hospitals and schools
while others fight to preserve traditional lifestyles. Equally, tigers are sensitive and the reason
many conservationists believe human-free core zones are essential to conserve apex predators.
A national mission to protect tigers on scientific terms needs to ensure such tracts.
Fundamentally, while a national policy protects rights, fine-grained mechanisms sensitive to
particular local conditions are crucial for people and tigers to sustainably coexist. Such
mechanisms are however beyond the ability of top-level Ministries. The conservation
establishment is likely to resist the new policy because it could slow efforts to consolidate tiger
habitats and increase the implementation burden, potentially leading to dual policies on the
ground. In fact, conservation in India is largely controlled by Forest Departments under the

where local departments wield significant control, forced relocations may continue in States

area for a sustainable population, their implementation often violates established principles.

should not mean entering one in which India’s natural riches can be forsworn.

II. Have you ever slept through your alarm and had to skip breakfast? Have you ever wished
for more protein in the morning than what bland oatmeal could provide? Have you ever been
stranded in the woods, starving, with nothing but a raw egg? If you answered “yes” to at least
one of these questions, Lenny Livingston could have helped. You see, Lenny had a superpower.

…Well, it was less a superpower, and more a “specific issue resolver.”

Lenny Livingston could [insert drumroll here] fry an egg under any circumstances, provided
he had a frying pan handy. No, he couldn’t create fire to heat the pan. No, he didn’t have laser
vision to cook the egg. And, no, he didn’t switch the uncooked egg for a fried one when you
weren’t looking. He merely cracked the egg open, dropped it into the pan, and shook his fist at
it threateningly. Moments later, the egg was so perfectly fried, Gordan Ramsay himself would
call it “the most amazing” thing he’d ever eaten (before remarking the burnt toast that came
with it was “a real shame”). Then, one day, after frying an egg more from frustration than
because he was hungry, Lenny found a note in his pocket:

TOP SECRET! You are cordially invited to join The Super Pals @ 12 Chestnut Drive, 7pm
tonight. Knock three times. Tell no one.

How the note had gotten into Lenny’s pocket was a mystery. He’d been home all day and hadn’t
seen anyone. His pants were fresh out of the dryer. Clearly, whoever had put it there must have
had some great superpower, like invisibility or super speed! At 7pm, Lenny skipped all the way
to the noted address (a modest rowhome within the city) and knocked upon the door. An elderly
woman in a nightgown greeted him. Not exactly the guard he’d been expecting. “I’m here to
see The Super Pals,” Lenny whispered.

“Eh?” the woman said. “Speak up, sonny.”

Lenny cleared his throat. “The Super Pals.”

“There’s a gas station down the street,” she said. “They have a commode. First stop on the trail.
Restroom’s for customers only, though, so you’ll have to buy something.”

“Ma!” someone from within shouted. “Who is it?”

“Another pedestrian on the Pooper Trail, Steven. Never you mind. Go back to playing dragon
dungeons with your friends.”

“I’m here to join up,” Lenny called inside. “The Super Pals.”

There was a thunderous stamping up the steps. Steven – a greasy, heavy-set fellow – appeared
and pulled Lenny in. “Shh! What if someone heard you! Didn’t you read the note? Top secret!”

The woman groaned. “Fine. But wash your hands when you’re done. And don’t tell me you
always do. We’ll both know it’s a lie.”

III. Can a person be charged for trying to create discord between religious communities with
“unsaid words”? In a deeply troubling decision, the Allahabad High Court recently said that a
WhatsApp text can indeed give a “subtle message” to stoke interfaith strife, even without
explicitly mentioning religion. It refused to quash an FIR and directed the accused, Afaq
Ahmad, to face trial. The decision could have a chilling effect on free speech.

Ahmad had moved the HC after the Uttar Pradesh police had registered a case against him
under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita’s Section 352 — it criminalises intentional insults that
provoke a breach of public peace. The police had sought to incriminate Ahmad on the basis of
a WhatsApp text to two people. Ahmad’s lawyers argued that their client only intended to
convey resentment about his brother’s arrest. The HC, however, said that the Whatsapp text,
“definitely conveys an underlying and subtle message that his brother has been targeted in a
false case, because of his belonging to a particular religious community.” It went on to say,
“even if one were to think that no religious feelings of a class of citizens or community have
been outraged… it is certainly a message, which, by its unsaid words, is likely to create or
promote feelings of enmity, hatred and ill-will between religious communities… members of
a particular community, in the first instance, could think that they are being targeted by
members of another religious community by abusing the process of law”.

Criminal laws, especially those that deal with the fundamental Right to Freedom of Speech and
Expression, require a clinical interpretation. In looking for unsaid words and subtle messaging,
the HC seems to have gone against the Supreme Court’s landmark 2015 ruling in Shreya
Singhal v Union of India. The apex court had said that “a penal law is void for vagueness if it
fails to define the criminal offence with sufficient definiteness”. It had underlined that
“ordinary people should be able to understand what conduct is prohibited and what is
permitted”. The Allahabad HC verdict, in contrast, frames a vague unlawful zone that people
must steer clear of. It goes against Shreya Singhal’s strictures against the “arbitrary and
discriminatory enforcement of the law”. The HC must course correct.

unsaid-words-allahabad-hc-anti-free-speech-10328459/
