III. Can a person be charged for trying to create discord between religious communities with
“unsaid words”? In a deeply troubling decision, the Allahabad High Court recently said that a
WhatsApp text can indeed give a “subtle message” to stoke interfaith strife, even without
explicitly mentioning religion. It refused to quash an FIR and directed the accused, Afaq
Ahmad, to face trial. The decision could have a chilling effect on free speech.

Ahmad had moved the HC after the Uttar Pradesh police had registered a case against him
under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita’s Section 352 — it criminalises intentional insults that
provoke a breach of public peace. The police had sought to incriminate Ahmad on the basis of
a WhatsApp text to two people. Ahmad’s lawyers argued that their client only intended to
convey resentment about his brother’s arrest. The HC, however, said that the Whatsapp text,
“definitely conveys an underlying and subtle message that his brother has been targeted in a
false case, because of his belonging to a particular religious community.” It went on to say,
“even if one were to think that no religious feelings of a class of citizens or community have
been outraged… it is certainly a message, which, by its unsaid words, is likely to create or
promote feelings of enmity, hatred and ill-will between religious communities… members of
a particular community, in the first instance, could think that they are being targeted by
members of another religious community by abusing the process of law”.

Criminal laws, especially those that deal with the fundamental Right to Freedom of Speech and
Expression, require a clinical interpretation. In looking for unsaid words and subtle messaging,
the HC seems to have gone against the Supreme Court’s landmark 2015 ruling in Shreya
Singhal v Union of India. The apex court had said that “a penal law is void for vagueness if it
fails to define the criminal offence with sufficient definiteness”. It had underlined that
“ordinary people should be able to understand what conduct is prohibited and what is
permitted”. The Allahabad HC verdict, in contrast, frames a vague unlawful zone that people
must steer clear of. It goes against Shreya Singhal’s strictures against the “arbitrary and
discriminatory enforcement of the law”. The HC must course correct.

IV. Women's work often gets obscured by omission—and science is one such fallow field.

for schools to reverse this trend. Though many may know about Marie Curie’s Nobel in physics
or even poet Byron’s daughter Ada Lovelace’s recognition as one of the earliest computer
programmers, few Indian students know of Indian women scientists. It’s not for a dearth in
their achievements. Whether it is chemist Asima Chatterjee’s seminal contribution in


developing anti-epileptic drugs, botanist Janaki Ammal’s work on plant breeding, or
biochemist Kamala Sohonie’s contribution towards understanding nutrition needs of the
poorest Indians, there is a wealth of icons to choose from. Such knowledge might just set off a
spark that lights India’s scientific journey ahead.

V. Supreme Court has sought govt support to frame norms to compensate for wrongful arrest,
prosecution and conviction. It announced its intent as it overturned the conviction of a man on
death row for six years. SC has frequently acquitted death row convicts and expressed its anger
and distress at subpar and dishonest police work and prosecution. It has berated subordinate
courts for wrong judgments. SC’s intent is welcome but must be seen to completion. This gap
in our justice system has been discussed threadbare. The Law Commission made its
recommendations (2018) while a legislative attempt in Lok Sabha – a private member’s bill,
the Protection of Rights of Wrongful Convicts Bill (2019) – lapsed. BNS was an opportunity
missed to put a compensation framework for false arrests, detention and conviction on the
statute. Wrong imprisonment isn’t merely justice denied, but dignity destroyed, lives shattered
and faith in justice system irreparably damaged.

So, how should compensation be decided? Law Commission recommended considering the
offence’s seriousness, severity of punishment, length of detention, damage to health, harm to
reputation, and of course, loss of income and opportunities. Add legal fees. In 2014, New York
City paid $40mn to five black and Latino men wrongly convicted in their teens in 1989 for a
brutal attack on a NY jogger in Central Park. DNA forensics cleared them 25 years later. US’s
National Registry of Exonerations recorded 153 exonerations in 2023, of which “nearly 84%
were people of colour”, and who “lost 2,230 years collectively for crimes they did not
commit…” Between 1989, when the state-wise record was started, and 2023, New York state
had made a total payout of $322mn to those wrongfully incarcerated.

India does not even maintain a record of wrongful arrests, prosecutions or convictions. And
when compensation is provided, the amount is often paltry. Discharged in 1996, it took Isro
scientist Nambi Narayanan 20 years to win a compensation of ₹50L. SC said state can’t avoid
its “vicarious liability”. But in 1998, SC had awarded him ₹1L in damages. One is expected to
be simply grateful one’s free, even if broken and shattered.

SOURCE: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-editorials/not-guilty-not-enough/

attention to India’s long-running Left-Wing Extremism (LWE) challenge. Security agencies
have described the development as part of a broader pattern of declining insurgent capacity,
attributed to coordinated operations, infrastructure expansion, and targeted rehabilitation
policies. Government officials emphasize that surrender frameworks combine financial
incentives, vocational training, and reintegration measures aimed at encouraging militants to
abandon armed struggle. Analysts, however, caution that ideological networks and localized
grievances continue to sustain pockets of insurgency across certain forested and mineral-rich
regions. The episode highlights the evolving nature of counter-insurgency policy in India,
which increasingly integrates security responses with developmental initiatives. Experts
suggest that long-term resolution depends not only on tactical success but also on addressing
governance deficits, land rights disputes, and socio-economic disparities in affected districts.

IX. The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) marked a turning point in India’s freedom
struggle by transforming anti-colonial resistance into a mass political movement. Led by
Mahatma Gandhi, the campaign encouraged Indians to withdraw cooperation from British
institutions, including schools, courts, legislatures, and foreign goods markets. It witnessed
unprecedented participation from students, lawyers, peasants, and urban middle classes across
regions. The movement also coincided with the Khilafat agitation, reflecting attempts to forge
Hindu-Muslim political unity against colonial rule. However, the movement was abruptly
suspended following the Chauri Chaura incident in 1922, where violent clashes resulted in the
death of policemen. Despite its withdrawal, historians consider the movement crucial in
legitimising mass civil disobedience as a political tool and establishing Gandhi as the central
leader of the national movement.


Source: Bipan Chandra, India’s Struggle for Independence.

content.passageText:
X. The foundational legal maxim Nemo Iudex In Causa Sua, which holds that no person shall
be a judge in their own cause, constitutes a cardinal principle of natural justice and a bedrock
requirement for the rule of law. Its primary imperative is to secure impartial adjudication, but
its profound utility lies in its equal commitment to safeguarding the perception of fairness,
thereby maintaining public confidence in the judicial system. The principle operates not merely
to root out actual bias but to eliminate any reasonable suspicion thereof, recognizing that justice
must be seen to be done.

The application of this rule encompasses several distinct yet interrelated doctrines. Bias is
categorized as either actual, requiring direct proof of prejudice, or apparent, governed by the
pervasive “reasonable suspicion” test. This objective test inquires whether a fair-minded and
informed observer, apprised of all relevant circumstances, would perceive a real possibility of
bias. Grounds giving rise to such a suspicion are well-established and include any financial or
proprietary interest in the outcome, however minimal; personal relationships suggesting
friendship or animosity; prior involvement in the same matter as an advocate or investigator;

content.passageText:
XI. The constitutional landscape of Ladakh has been fundamentally altered since its
designation as a Union Territory without a legislature in 2019, spurring persistent demands for
statehood and inclusion under the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution. This movement
is rooted in legal and existential anxieties among the region's overwhelming tribal majority,
who fear the erosion of autonomous governance and the absence of robust constitutional
safeguards. The Sixth Schedule, enshrined in Articles 244(2) and 275(1), represents a dedicated
framework for tribal self-rule, originally formulated from the Bardoloi Committee's
recommendations to protect distinct social, cultural, and land rights within the broader union.
It provides for the creation of Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) and Autonomous
Regional Councils (ARCs) by the Governor, granting them substantive legislative, judicial,
executive, and financial powers to govern local affairs.

For Ladakh, the appeal of this schedule lies in its potential to address multifaceted grievances.
The loss of representative government post-2019 has centralized authority in bureaucratic
hands, heightening concerns over land alienation, demographic change, and cultural dilution,
especially following alterations to domicile policies. Legally, the schedule empowers ADCs to
enact laws on critical subjects like land, forests, agriculture, and social customs, subject to
gubernatorial assent, and to adjudicate tribal disputes through dedicated courts. Executive
functions include managing local infrastructure and resources, while financial autonomy
permits revenue generation through taxes and levies. Such powers are deemed essential to
shield Ladakh’s fragile ecology from unregulated tourism and development, and to align
economic planning with local needs amid high unemployment.

However, conferring Sixth Schedule status entails significant legal complexities.
Constitutionally, its application beyond the northeastern region necessitates an amendment, as


the provision was historically tailored for those specific tribal contexts. Security imperatives
in a sensitive border area raise questions about coordinating defense and administration with
autonomous bodies. Administratively, experiences from existing ADCs reveal challenges like
financial dependency on central funds and political interference, which could undermine
efficacy. Moreover, granting such autonomy may create precedents, inviting similar demands
from other tribal regions and testing the balance between decentralized governance and
uniform national policy. While interim measures like job reservations and linguistic promotions
have been instituted, they are perceived as insufficient substitutes for the comprehensive legal
protection offered by the Sixth Schedule, framing a pivotal constitutional debate on tribal
autonomy and integration.

content.passageText:
XII. The Indian Penal Code, 1860, designates offences against the state’s very existence as its
most severe crimes, encapsulated in Chapter VI. At its apex lies Section 121, which
criminalizes the act of waging, attempting to wage, or abetting the waging of war against the
Government of India. This provision targets not mere disorder but collective violence of a
political character aimed at overthrowing the government or coercing it by force. The essence
of "waging war" distinguishes it from riots or isolated rebellions; it requires an assembly with
a public, general purpose and a force sufficient to challenge the state’s sovereignty. An
illustrative example is an armed insurrection to seize a government arsenal with the goal of
subverting constitutional authority. Given its gravity, the punishment is extraordinarily
stringent: death or imprisonment for life, coupled with a fine and mandatory forfeiture of
property.

Recognizing that the gravest threats often begin in secret, the law proactively targets conspiracy
through Section 121A. This section penalizes the very agreement to commit offences under
Section 121, criminalizing the planning stage before any overt act of violence materializes. The
key ingredient is a conspiracy between two or more persons either to wage war or to deprive
India of its sovereignty. Thus, the state need not wait for an uprising; the plot itself is punishable
by imprisonment for life or up to ten years, and a fine.

Further along the continuum of preparation, Section 122 addresses the tangible steps taken
towards this end. It punishes collecting arms, ammunition, or otherwise preparing to wage war,
provided such acts are done with the specific intention of using them against the state. This
moves beyond conspiracy into actionable preparation, meriting a similarly severe punishment
of life imprisonment or up to ten years, and a fine.

Finally, Section 123 casts a wide net by criminalizing the concealment of a design to wage war.
An individual who, knowing of such a treasonous design, actively conceals it with the intent
to facilitate its execution, becomes complicit. This offence underscores the legal duty not to
aid such plots through silence or deception, punishable by imprisonment up to ten years and a
fine.

Collectively, these sections form a formidable legal bulwark. They protect state stability by
addressing the entire spectrum of treasonous activity—from the ultimate act of war, through
its conspiracy and preparation, down to its intentional concealment—ensuring that both action
and treacherous intent are met with the full force of the law.

content.passageText:
XIII. The Indian legal system's approach to environmental protection represents a dynamic
interplay between constitutional mandates, legislative action, and proactive judicial
interpretation. This framework has evolved from a reactive, penalty-based model to one
increasingly focused on prevention, sustainability, and the recognition of ecological rights. The
foundation is significantly bolstered by constitutional amendments that inserted specific
directives for the state and duties for citizens towards environmental protection, providing a
bedrock for expansive judicial construction.

A critical feature of this landscape is the role of the judiciary in formulating and applying
overarching doctrinal principles that guide administrative and legislative action. The courts
have moved beyond mere textual interpretation to embed concepts such as Sustainable
Development, which mandates a balance between economic advancement and ecological
integrity. Complementing this is the rigorous Precautionary Principle, which places the burden
of proof regarding environmental safety on the proponent of a potentially harmful project,
especially in the face of scientific uncertainty. Furthermore, the Absolute Liability principle
imposes stringent responsibility on industries engaged in inherently hazardous activities for


any consequent environmental damage, ensuring accountability transcends traditional fault-
based legal reasoning.

At the institutional level, specialized adjudicatory bodies have been established to provide
expedited and expert resolution of environmental disputes, operating alongside traditional civil
and criminal justice mechanisms. Concurrently, a suite of legislations addresses specific media
like air and water, while a broader umbrella act empowers the central government to formulate
delegated rules on diverse issues from waste management to ecological sensitivity. This
complex legal architecture is continuously tested by contemporary challenges like climate
change, which is pushing the boundaries of existing laws and prompting calls for more
integrated governance that views a healthy ecosystem as an indispensable prerequisite for the
fulfillment of fundamental human rights and equitable development.

content.passageText:
XIV. Judicial review of administrative action constitutes the cornerstone of India’s
constitutional framework for ensuring governmental accountability and upholding the rule of
law. As the core mechanism to check administrative excesses, it empowers constitutional courts
to scrutinize the legality, rationality, and procedural propriety of executive decisions. This
supervisory jurisdiction, inherent under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution, is not an appeal
on merits but a review of the decision-making process itself, ensuring that state power is
exercised within defined legal boundaries.

The grounds for such review are well-established. Firstly, jurisdictional error occurs when an
authority acts without jurisdiction, in excess of it, or fails to exercise a jurisdiction it possesses.
Secondly, an error of law apparent on the face of the record allows courts to intervene where a
clear legal flaw is discernible from the order itself, without delving into intricate evidence.
Thirdly, while factual findings are typically respected, courts will intervene in cases of an error
in finding of fact where the conclusion is so perverse that no reasonable person could have
arrived at it, or is based on no evidence whatsoever.

The principles of natural justice—audi alteram partem (hear the other side) and nemo judex in
causa sua (no one should be a judge in their own cause)—form a vital ground. Any decision
violating these foundational tenets of fairness, such as acting with bias or denying a reasonable
hearing, is rendered void. Furthermore, abuse or misuse of discretion is a critical check against
arbitrariness. Discretion must be exercised reasonably, for the purpose granted, without mala
fides, and considering all relevant factors; its misuse on irrelevant grounds or in a manifestly
unfair manner invites judicial correction. Finally, procedural ultra vires ensures that mandatory
statutory procedures are meticulously followed, as their breach invalidates the subsequent
action.

Thus, judicial review operates as an essential democratic safeguard. It balances administrative
efficiency with individual rights, ensuring that public power is exercised in a manner that is
neither beyond authority nor contrary to justice, thereby reinforcing constitutional governance.

arrived at it, or is based on no evidence whatsoever.

The principles of natural justice—audi alteram partem (hear the other side) and nemo judex in
causa sua (no one should be a judge in their own cause)—form a vital ground. Any decision
violating these foundational tenets of fairness, such as acting with bias or denying a reasonable
hearing, is rendered void. Furthermore, abuse or misuse of discretion is a critical check against
arbitrariness. Discretion must be exercised reasonably, for the purpose granted, without mala
fides, and considering all relevant factors; its misuse on irrelevant grounds or in a manifestly
unfair manner invites judicial correction. Finally, procedural ultra vires ensures that mandatory
statutory procedures are meticulously followed, as their breach invalidates the subsequent
action.

Thus, judicial review operates as an essential democratic safeguard. It balances administrative
efficiency with individual rights, ensuring that public power is exercised in a manner that is
neither beyond authority nor contrary to justice, thereby reinforcing constitutional governance.

law. As the core mechanism to check administrative excesses, it empowers constitutional courts

content.passageText:
XV. The Basic Structure Doctrine represents a seminal and transformative principle in Indian
constitutional jurisprudence, marking a profound evolution in the understanding of sovereign
power and constitutional permanence. Its genesis lies in the interpretative journey of the
Supreme Court, which grappled with the seemingly absolute amending power granted to
Parliament under Article 368. The doctrine emerged not from a specific constitutional clause,
but as a judicial construct derived from a holistic reading of the Constitution’s spirit, its
historical context, and its overarching architecture. It establishes that while Parliament has the
authority to amend any part of the Constitution, this power does not extend to altering or
destroying its fundamental, essential features.

This judicial principle was crystallized in the landmark 1973 ruling, which settled a previously
unresolved constitutional question. The decision signified a pivotal shift from a more textual
interpretation, thereby creating a substantive limitation on the amendment power. The doctrine
serves as a constitutional bedrock, ensuring that the identity of the founding document remains
intact through the dynamic processes of change and adaptation. It underscores the Constitution
as a living instrument of governance, not merely a statute subject to the transient will of a
parliamentary majority.

The content of the basic structure is not a closed or exhaustive list but has been elucidated
through subsequent judicial pronouncements over decades. The Supreme Court has, in various
cases, identified and affirmed several elements as constituting this inviolable core. These
features are considered fundamental to the constitutional vision and the democratic republic it
establishes. The doctrine’s enforcement inherently involves judicial review of constitutional
amendments, placing the judiciary in the role of the ultimate guardian of the Constitution’s
essential framework. This interpretive mechanism ensures a delicate balance between the
principles of parliamentary sovereignty, judicial review, and constitutional supremacy. It
embodies the conviction that the Constitution possesses an enduring identity that transcends
ordinary political processes, safeguarding the foundational promises made to the people of
India. The doctrine thus acts as a counterweight, preserving the core values of the constitutional
order from abrogation under the guise of legal amendment.

content.passageText:
XVI. Now digital platforms are ending the broadcast era. Just over 15 million people watched
England lose to Spain in the final of Euro 2024; the podcaster Joe Rogan has more than 14
million followers on Spotify alone, and another 20 million subscribers on YouTube. Rogan’s
reach is global, but there are scores of minor influencers producing weekly or daily YouTube
shows that attract audiences that rival and even surpass the nightly viewership for BBC News
at Six. This is the era of posting.

The shift is not just a matter of where people get their information (or disinformation): the
online world is where we build communities, debate and shape ideologies and policy. Digital
platforms alter the form and style of these discussions. Online, whether to drink tap water can
be as political as whether to reduce net migration; posting edgy content can shape policy faster
than joining a protest; and the appeal of politics is less about meeting material interests than
finding what feels authentic amid the fakes, filters and AI slop.

The churn of social media acts as a kind of undertow, pulling political conversations toward
ideas and tropes that attract enough engagement to rise to the surface of the attention economy.
Traditional political communications, with its emphasis on focus group-vetted messaging,
either gets washed away or it becomes fodder for mockery, trolling and conspiracy theorising.
The institutional gatekeepers have fallen, replaced by influencers who succeed by navigating
the fickle currents of audience attention.

On X, Elon Musk has re-platformed figures such as Nick Fuentes – white supremacist and
antisemitic livestreamer – who now has half as many X followers as Keir Starmer. The recently
reinstated Andrew Tate’s follower count exceeds the prime minister’s by 9 million. Labour
would probably highlight its focus on delivering sensible policies instead of posting online, but
as a result it has stumbled into a conspiratorial rat’s nest with its digital ID policy.

In contrast, Reform UK is riding the wave, posting content attuned to ever-changing trends on
platforms such as TikTok, where its leader, Nigel Farage, has more followers than all other
MPs combined. Like all good influencers, he flogs merch and posts videos of himself either
vibing out or “owning” journalists. His audience turns these into supercuts set to “phonk”
music, a subgenre of Memphis hip-hop co-opted by online reactionaries.

[Extracted with revisions and edits from “How liberals lost the internet”, The Guardian.]

content.passageText:
XIX. Following the release of the US National Security Strategy in November 2025, the Trump
administration—led by the US Department of Defense, now rechristened as the Department of
War—unveiled the unclassified 2026 US National Defense Strategy. In characteristically
Trumpian fashion, the latest NDS opens with a blunt assault on America’s post-Cold War
foreign policy establishment.

“America emerged from the Cold War as the world’s most powerful nation by a wide margin.
We were secure in our hemisphere, with a military that was focused on warfighting and far
superior to anyone else’s, engaged allies, and powerful industry,” it says. But in the same
breath, it contends, “But rather than husband and cultivate these hard-earned advantages, our
nation’s post–Cold War leadership and foreign policy establishment squandered them.”

The NDS takes a direct aim at previous administrations for operating under the illusion that the
United States could simultaneously deter great powers, stabilise regions, fight terrorism,
reassure allies, and uphold a global order.

While both the NDS of 2018 during Trump’s first term and the 2022 NDS of the Biden
administration did reflect the mounting strain on America’s resources created by such an
expansive agenda, the latest strategy makes a radical break. It openly seeks to end what the
Trump administration characterises as persistent free-riding by allies and partners on US global
commitments. It signals a deliberate contraction of America’s global ambitions, a sharper
prioritisation of interests, and an explicit ranking of threats.

The 2018 National Defense Strategy marked a decisive break from the post-9/11 era. It elevated
great-power competition over counter-terrorism and explicitly cast China and Russia as “near-
peer competitors” challenging US primacy. However, its ambition remained global, reinforcing
alliance commitments and sustained US engagement within the existing international order.

The Biden administration’s 2022 NDS carried this shift forward but wrapped it within a more
ideological narrative of “democracies vs autocracies”. It emphasised the operationalisation of
“integrated deterrence”, solidifying alliance networks, and the defence of a “rules-based
order”. It saw the world through a lens of interconnected, universal threats and not prioritisation
of specific ones.


[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Trump made it clear that US military isn’t global
police with National Defence Strategy 2026”, ThePrint.]

              requiring troop deployments abroad.

All prior administrations knowingly pursued policies that would weaken
              America’s global standing over the long term.

The previous approach actively hampers effectively countering today’s
              primary identified dangers.

content.passageText:
I. The Supreme Court judgement on the right to menstrual hygiene as an integral part of the
constitutional right to life and dignity provides a long-desired direction towards destigmatising
an essential bodily function and ensuring basic care. While observing that the lack of basic
facilities and the stigma around menstruation directly affect girls’ health, education and privacy,
the bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and R Mahadevan directed all states and Union territories
to ensure within three months that every school has gender-segregated toilets, and
biodegradable or reusable sanitary pads are provided for free to adolescent girls along with safe
disposal facilities. The court also asked the governments to incorporate gender-responsive
curriculums in schools and train the staff in assisting menstruating pupils.
The apex court’s judgement and directions expose the socio-cultural and religious taboos
perpetuated by patriarchal norms. Period shame is every girl’s burden. The event of puberty, a
milestone in human physiological evolution, is celebrated in many Indian traditions. But period
ostracisation is so deeply prevalent in many sections that the victims of such misinformed
belief and gender aggression are eventually socialised to become its carriers. The troubling
apportioning of ‘shame’ continues through generations. For girls born into economically
weaker families, sanitary pads are a luxury. Government schools, an ideal place to clear the
misconceptions for both girls and boys, ignore this duty. To aggravate the insensitive attitude,
their administrators often force hapless teenage girls to explain clothes stains as period blood,
stripping them of dignity.
By one estimate, around 2.3 crore girls drop out of school annually on account of lack of
adequate toilets and menstrual provisions. The launch of the Union Health Ministry’s
Menstrual Hygiene Scheme in 2011 was a landmark attempt to destigmatise menstruation by
giving girls aged 10 to 19 subsidised pads and menstrual education. But it left out the adolescent
girls who are out of school. The right to education is as fundamental a right as the right to live
with dignity. With the Supreme Court spelling out the nuances of the constitutional right of
young girls in detail, it’s time to fill the gaps. For that, government and private schools have to
act in a timebound manner. And all three tiers of government have to ensure that awareness of
the right as well as the health basics reach all sections of India—in every generation.
SOURCE:https://www.newindianexpress.com/editorial/2026/Feb/08/menstruation-rights-as-
institutional-assurance

an essential bodily function and ensuring basic care. While observing that the lack of basic
facilities and the stigma around menstruation directly affect girls’ health, education and privacy,
the bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and R Mahadevan directed all states and Union territories
to ensure within three months that every school has gender-segregated toilets, and
biodegradable or reusable sanitary pads are provided for free to adolescent girls along with safe
disposal facilities. The court also asked the governments to incorporate gender-responsive
curriculums in schools and train the staff in assisting menstruating pupils.
The apex court’s judgement and directions expose the socio-cultural and religious taboos
perpetuated by patriarchal norms. Period shame is every girl’s burden. The event of puberty, a
milestone in human physiological evolution, is celebrated in many Indian traditions. But period
ostracisation is so deeply prevalent in many sections that the victims of such misinformed
belief and gender aggression are eventually socialised to become its carriers. The troubling
apportioning of ‘shame’ continues through generations. For girls born into economically
weaker families, sanitary pads are a luxury. Government schools, an ideal place to clear the
misconceptions for both girls and boys, ignore this duty. To aggravate the insensitive attitude,
their administrators often force hapless teenage girls to explain clothes stains as period blood,
stripping them of dignity.
By one estimate, around 2.3 crore girls drop out of school annually on account of lack of
adequate toilets and menstrual provisions. The launch of the Union Health Ministry’s
Menstrual Hygiene Scheme in 2011 was a landmark attempt to destigmatise menstruation by
giving girls aged 10 to 19 subsidised pads and menstrual education. But it left out the adolescent
girls who are out of school. The right to education is as fundamental a right as the right to live
with dignity. With the Supreme Court spelling out the nuances of the constitutional right of
young girls in detail, it’s time to fill the gaps. For that, government and private schools have to
act in a timebound manner. And all three tiers of government have to ensure that awareness of
the right as well as the health basics reach all sections of India—in every generation.

II. There was commotion in Roaring Camp. It could not have been a fight, for in 1850 that was
not novel enough to have called together the entire settlement. The ditches and claims were not
only deserted, but "Tuttle's grocery" had contributed its gamblers, who, it will be remembered,
calmly continued their game the day that French Pete and Kanaka Joe shot each other to death
over the bar in the front room. The whole camp was collected before a rude cabin on the outer
edge of the clearing. Conversation was carried on in a low tone, but the name of a woman was
frequently repeated. It was a name familiar enough in the camp,—"Cherokee Sal."
Perhaps the less said of her the better. She was a coarse and, it is to be feared, a very sinful
woman. But at that time she was the only woman in Roaring Camp, and was just then lying in
sore extremity when she most needed the ministration of her own sex. Dissolute, abandoned,
and irreclaimable, she was yet suffering a martyrdom hard enough to bear even when veiled by
sympathizing womanhood, but now terrible in her loneliness. The primal curse had come to
her in that original isolation which must have made the punishment of the first transgression
so dreadful. It was, perhaps, part of the expiation of her sin that, at a moment when she most
lacked her sex's intuitive tenderness and care, she met only the half-contemptuous faces of her
masculine associates. Yet a few of the spectators were, I think, touched by her sufferings. Sandy
Tipton thought it was "rough on Sal," and, in the contemplation of her condition, for a moment
rose superior to the fact that he had an ace and two bowers in his sleeve.
It will be seen also that the situation was novel. Deaths were by no means uncommon in
Roaring Camp, but a birth was a new thing. People had been dismissed the camp effectively,
finally, and with no possibility of return; but this was the first time that anybody had been
introduced ab initio. Hence the excitement.
"You go in there, Stumpy," said a prominent citizen known as "Kentuck," addressing one of
the loungers. "Go in there, and see what you kin do. You've had experience in them things."
Perhaps there was a fitness in the selection. Stumpy, in other climes, had been the putative head
of two families; in fact, it was owing to some legal informality in these proceedings that
Roaring Camp—a city of refuge—was indebted to his company. The crowd approved the
choice, and Stumpy was wise enough to bow to the majority. The door closed on the extempore
surgeon and midwife, and Roaring Camp sat down outside, smoked its pipe, and awaited the
issue.

III. There is a sudden meltdown across different asset classes around the world—barring
equities, which have escaped the turmoil till now. Silver and gold, which saw a historic rise in
prices in 2025, have come under pressure of late. The price escalation seen last year proved
ephemeral as silver crashed from a peak of $125 an ounce in the last week of January to a low
of $70 before closing around $77.
The virtual currency market is witnessing its share of volatility—a trend not unfamiliar to this
asset class. Bitcoin is down 44 percent since its October peak of $125,000, while Ethereum has
fallen 56 percent from its August peak of $4,800. The sharp rise and fall in bullion and
cryptocurrencies are closely associated with uncertainty around US-led trade policies. At a
granular level, there are specific reasons for the degree of decline in each asset class.
The lack of clarity on their regulatory status has weighed on cryptos even as institutional buying
has picked up. The fall in gold and silver can be linked to the lower uncertainty around US
trade policy than in 2025. Additionally, the US government’s nomination of Kevin Warsh for
the Fed chair has had a cooling effect on bullion. Warsh is expected to be less aggressive with
rate cuts, fuelling bearish sentiment in both gold and silver. This has led to large-scale outflows
from gold and silver exchange-traded funds, further reinforcing the bearish trend.
The unexpected rise in silver prices in 2025 was attributed to a growing demand-supply gap.
Industrial use of silver has been rising, with demand from the solar energy and electronics
sectors soaring. But at these price levels, the supply gap is expected to shrink, with demand for
investment and jewellery likely to fall in 2026. Irrespective of the steady industrial demand for
silver and other metals such as copper, such steep price rises are unsustainable beyond.
Investors who missed the metals rally in 2025 should not expect a similar run in 2026. The
‘irrational’ expectation of an encore from these metals should therefore be viewed with caution.
Silver and copper are not the new gold, nor are virtual currencies. These are volatile asset
classes, and investors should not treat an exceptional run in any of these as the new normal.

IV. The “ultimate answer to life, the universe and everything”, wrote Douglas Adams in The
Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, is “42”. Or, in other words, the product of six and seven.
There’s one minor snag: No one quite knows what the ultimate question is. In much the same
way, it appears, no adult quite knows what “six-seven” — the newest cultural mayfly that
teens around the world, including in India, are dropping like confetti in classrooms,
playgrounds and at the dining table — means. That is the entire point.
Neologisms of such variety have always marked the boundaries of youth — encrypted codes
incomprehensible to adults, insouciant to friends, and doomed to obsolescence. The internet
has turbocharged this cycle, turning slang into cultural currency traded across reels and clips,
on Instagram and Discord servers. Once upon a timeline, things were “on fleek”. Then came
“yeet” and “slay”. Before that, everything was “lit” and YOLO, miles above “mid”. “Skibidi”
came and went in the space of a meme. “Six-seven” has followed the same pattern of digital
migration. It appears to have sprouted from a 2024 rap track, ‘Doot Doot’ (6 7) by Skrilla,
before mutating through basketball fandom, mostly of LaMelo Ball, 6ft 7in — but of course
— and landing in an episode of South Park. Along the way, it also acquired a visual meme
code: Upturned palms, rising and falling in tandem.
The freedom of such coinages has always been in their ephemerality: A flare of rebellion
against the grammar police, a reminder that language, like adolescence, can be play —
elastic, irreverent and gloriously incomprehensible to those who pay the WiFi bill — before
maturing into something entirely mundane. The other surest way to kill a trend, of course, is
to have parents use it. Or worse, wear it. In the United States this Halloween, “six-seven”
costumes are reportedly gaining traction among parents, much to the agony of their offspring.
Because nothing says the death of cool quite like dad wearing it.

V. It can look like garbage and act like garbage but litter is something different – garbage placed
where it shouldn’t be. As popular as this activity is among us Indians we were aghast to learn
that a lady walking about outer London was fined £150 for it. All she had done was pour the
last of her coffee down a drain. She hadn’t even thrown her mug in. It was reusable. Nearer us,


in Singapore littering fines can go up to S$2,000 – and to S$10,000 beyond the third conviction.
If our governments went about fining litterers so liberally, the collection could put GST
revenues to shame.
Why are Indians so fond of littering? We see a choking river, we worsen its misery. We see a
pristine one, we introduce it to plastic bags, paper napkins, rubber chappals. Sometimes we
throw the half-eaten burger right next to a wastebin. My one chewing gum wrapper won’t make
a difference, our demon self whispers. Except it’s joined by a hundred, thousand, million others,
and it makes all the difference.
We loooove to holiday in Japan but guess what helps make it so holidayable? People carry their
trash home rather than spray it about. We cleaned our homes thoroughly on Diwali but spread
its detritus across our parks and streets. Cleaning all that is someone else’s job, we think. But
if we want to live in a clean society, we too have to stop doing the dirty.
SOURCE: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-editorials/litter-bugs/

content.passageText:
X. The Sale of Goods Act establishes a foundational commercial framework by distinguishing
between two pivotal types of contractual terms: conditions and warranties. A condition is a
fundamental term central to the contract's identity, the breach of which entitles the aggrieved
party to treat the contract as repudiated, reject the goods, and claim damages. In contrast, a
warranty is a subsidiary or collateral promise, breach of which only grants a right to damages,
not termination. This distinction is critical as it dictates the available remedies, ensuring
proportionality between the breach's gravity and the legal recourse.
Regarding stipulations as to time, the Act provides clarity on contractual performance
deadlines. Unless a different intention is expressly stated or necessarily implied from the
contract's circumstances, time of payment is not deemed to be "of the essence." However, time
for delivery may be construed as a condition if the commercial context or explicit agreement
indicates its fundamental importance, allowing rejection for delayed performance.
The Act's most significant contribution lies in its implied conditions and warranties, which
operate as core statutory protections. These terms are automatically woven into every sales
contract unless explicitly excluded. Primarily, there is an implied condition on title: that the
seller has the legal right to sell the goods. Further, where goods are sold by description, there
is a condition that they will correspond materially with that description. Critically, goods must
be of satisfactory quality—considering their price, description, and durability—and be
reasonably fit for any particular purpose the buyer made known to the seller, implying reliance
on the seller's skill or judgment. Finally, in a sale by sample, implied conditions stipulate that
the bulk will correspond with the sample in quality, and that the buyer will have a reasonable
opportunity to compare the two, safeguarding against latent defects not apparent in the sample.
Collectively, these provisions create a balanced legal architecture, protecting buyers from
deficient performance while providing sellers with clear standards, thereby facilitating fair and
predictable commercial exchange.

content.passageText:
XI. The constitutional framework of India vests in the judiciary the formidable power to issue
prerogative writs, a cornerstone of judicial review and fundamental rights enforcement.
Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution empower the Supreme Court and High Courts,
respectively, to issue writs such as Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo
Warranto. These remedies, deeply rooted in English common law, have been meticulously
adapted to serve as essential instruments for upholding the rule of law and constitutional
morality in a democratic republic. Their evolution reflects a dynamic jurisprudence that
responds to societal needs while safeguarding liberty and accountability.
Historically, writs originated as royal commands, but in India, they have transformed into
judicial orders that curtail executive and legislative excesses. Each writ serves a distinct
function: Habeas Corpus secures personal liberty against unlawful detention; Mandamus
compels public authorities to perform legal duties; Certiorari quashes orders passed without
jurisdiction; Prohibition prevents such proceedings; and Quo Warranto scrutinizes the right to
hold public office. Collectively, they form a robust mechanism for constitutional redress,
ensuring that state power is exercised within legal boundaries.
The interpretation and scope of these writs have expanded significantly through judicial
innovation. The rise of Public Interest Litigation (PIL) liberalized standing rules, allowing
courts to address systemic issues affecting communities. This development particularly
influenced Mandamus, evolving it into a tool for "continuing mandamus," where courts issue


ongoing directions and monitor compliance, especially in areas like environmental protection.
Similarly, Habeas Corpus has been broadly construed to protect not merely physical freedom
but also the right to live with dignity under Article 21. Even during periods of constitutional
strain, such as emergencies, the judiciary has navigated the suspension of rights, affirming the
resilience of writ jurisdiction as a shield against arbitrariness.
Landmark rulings, such as L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), reinforce that judicial
review via writs is a basic feature of the Constitution, immutable and inviolable. This principle
ensures that constitutional courts retain supervisory authority over tribunals, maintaining a
hierarchy of justice and preventing the ouster of fundamental safeguards. Thus, writs are not
static remedies but living instruments that adapt to contemporary challenges, balancing
individual freedoms with state authority. They embody the judiciary's role as the guardian of
the Constitution, continuously interpreting legal norms to preserve democratic values and
ensure justice remains accessible and substantive in an ever-evolving polity.
content.questionText:

       the right to move any court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Article
       19 and others. However, which writ remains maintainable even during such suspension
       to challenge a detention order?

              preventive detention.

Habeas Corpus, because the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21
              cannot be suspended.

Mandamus, to compel the detaining authority to follow the procedure
              established by law.

None of the above; all writs for enforcement of suspended rights become
              infructuous.

content.passageText:
XII. The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, incorporates strategic mechanisms to enhance
judicial efficiency while balancing the interests of justice. Two significant provisions in this
regard are Plea Bargaining and the Summary Procedure for compoundable and non-
compoundable offences, both designed to expedite the resolution of specific categories of
cases.
Plea Bargaining, introduced under Chapter XXI-A (Sections 265A-265L), represents a
transformative departure from conventional adversarial litigation. This judicially supervised


process allows an accused person to voluntarily plead guilty in exchange for a concession in
the nature or length of the sentence. However, its application is strictly limited to offences not
punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment exceeding seven years. It is also
excluded for offences affecting the socio-economic condition of the country or committed
against women or children below fourteen. The procedure is initiated by the accused filing an
application, after which the court, upon satisfaction of voluntariness, may provide time for a
mutually satisfactory disposition involving the victim. The resultant disposition, if reached,
leads to a report from the court and the award of a specified sentence, which may include
probation or a reduced term. This mechanism aims to unclog dockets, provide quicker
resolution to the accused, and ensure a measure of restitution for the victim.
Complementing this is the framework under Section 320 for the summary procedure
concerning compoundable and non-compoundable offences. Compoundable offences are those
where the victim or complainant can legally enter into a compromise, thereby withdrawing the
charges and terminating the prosecution. These are categorized into those compoundable
without the court's permission (e.g., simple hurt, adultery) and those requiring it (e.g., criminal
breach of trust, voluntarily causing grievous hurt). The act of compounding has the effect of an
acquittal. In contrast, non-compoundable offences, being graver in nature, cannot be settled
privately and must be prosecuted by the state. The summary procedure for trying petty cases,
as outlined in other CrPC provisions, allows Magistrates to try such offences following a swift
and simplified process, culminating in a prompt judgment. Together, these provisions on
compounding and summary trials allow the criminal justice system to allocate its resources
optimally, reserving lengthy, full-dress trials for serious crimes while permitting amicable or
expedited settlements for less severe transgressions.

              imprisonment exceeding seven years.

No, because theft is specifically excluded from plea bargaining as it affects the
              socio-economic condition of the country.

Yes, but only if the offence is also compoundable under Section 320 of the
              CrPC.

No, because the victim's willingness compromises the voluntary nature of the
              plea.

content.passageText:
XIII. The Indian constitutional framework is not merely a collection of articles but a dynamic
ecosystem sustained by a body of interpretive principles. These judicial doctrines, developed
over decades, serve as essential tools for navigating the complex interplay between different
constitutional mandates, legislative entries, and fundamental guarantees. They allow the
judiciary to perform its delicate role as the guardian of the constitutional scheme without
unduly encroaching upon the legislative domain. These principles often emerge from the
necessity to resolve apparent conflicts, whether between competing legislative powers of the
Union and the States, or between the state’s authority to make laws and the citizen’s inviolable
rights.
At the heart of this interpretive jurisprudence lies the need to balance federal architecture with
individual liberties. One key area involves assessing laws that appear to contradict foundational
freedoms granted by the Constitution. Here, the judiciary may examine whether such an archaic
law is permanently invalid or possesses a potential for future operation, a concept distinct from
total nullity. Similarly, in a federal system, disputes inevitably arise concerning which
legislature—Union or State—is competent to enact a particular law. To adjudicate such
disputes, courts often look beyond the apparent subject of a statute to its core purpose and
substantial effect, ensuring that legislatures operate within their constitutionally demarcated
spheres. This prevents legislative overreach where the form of a law masks a trespass into a
forbidden domain, a situation where the substance of the legislation is scrutinized against the
backdrop of the Seventh Schedule.
Furthermore, when a law enacted by a state legislature is challenged for purportedly affecting
matters beyond its territorial jurisdiction, the courts apply a principle to determine if a sufficient
connection exists between the state and the subject of the legislation. This ensures that state
laws having extra-territorial impact remain constitutionally sound. Ultimately, when two
constitutional provisions or statutory interpretations seem in tension, the guiding imperative is
to adopt a construction that reconciles them, preserving the integrity of the legal text and giving
effect to the holistic intent of the framers. Collectively, these doctrines embody the
constitutional ethos of equilibrium, ensuring a harmonious coexistence of power, liberty, and
federalism.

content.passageText:
XIV. Public nuisance is a distinct legal doctrine addressing an unreasonable and substantial
interference with a right common to the general public, such as health, safety, peace, or
convenience. Unlike a private nuisance, which protects an individual’s enjoyment of land, a
public nuisance defends communal rights. Classic examples include obstructing a public
highway, polluting a river used by the community, maintaining a house of prostitution, or
creating a public health hazard. Its character as a wrong against the public means it is frequently
both a crime, prosecutable by the state, and a tort, allowing for civil redress.
A critical and defining element of public nuisance law is the stringent requirement for standing
to sue. Historically, only the state, acting through the Attorney General, could bring suit to
abate a public nuisance. This reflected the principle that a wrong to the public should be
rectified by the public’s representative. The modern rule, however, permits a private citizen to
file a civil action, but only upon demonstrating a “special injury.” This harm must be
qualitatively different in kind, not merely greater in degree, from the inconvenience suffered
by the general public. For instance, while all citizens may be delayed by an illegally blocked
road, a shop owner whose sole access is cut off, causing unique and severe economic losses,
suffers the requisite special injury to pursue a claim.
The remedies available correspond to the party bringing the action. The primary remedy sought
by the state is an injunction—a court order compelling the defendant to cease the offending
activity. Public authorities may also exercise their power of abatement, directly removing the
nuisance (e.g., clearing an obstruction). For the private plaintiff who successfully proves both
the public nuisance and a special injury, the available remedy is compensatory damages for
their distinct losses. Thus, public nuisance law operates on two tiers: one for the protection of
the collective welfare and another, more narrow path, for redressing exceptional harm to private
individuals arising from that public wrong.

             standing to file a lawsuit.

             by the whole town.

             kind from the public's loss.

XV. The constitutional architecture governing elections in India establishes a robust framework
designed to uphold the integrity of the democratic process. At the heart of this framework lies
the Election Commission of India, a permanent and independent body constituted under Article
324 of the Constitution. The foundational principle embedded within this provision is the
vesting of "superintendence, direction, and control" of elections exclusively in this
Commission, a phrase that has been the subject of extensive judicial scrutiny to delineate its
vast and plenary scope. This constitutional entrustment is not merely administrative but is
imbued with the responsibility of ensuring elections that are free, fair, and reflective of the
genuine will of the electorate.
The Commission’s autonomy is safeguarded through a suite of constitutional and statutory

content.passageText:
XVIII. Don’t be fooled. When it comes to Donald Trump, what might look like a full retreat
is almost always a mere tactical withdrawal, designed to buy time. He’ll step back when he’s
forced to, under pressure, but will then revert the instant the pressure lets up. Too often, his
opponents, whether at home or abroad, allow themselves to be played, confusing a mere pause
for a surrender – and the risk is strong that they’re making that same mistake all over again.
This week, the US president won praise in some quarters for moving to “de-escalate” the war
he has been waging on the people of Minneapolis. Following the killing of Alex Pretti, an
intensive care nurse who posed no threat and yet was shot at least 10 times by masked agents
of Customs and Border Protection or CBP, Trump signalled that he wanted to calm things down.
He shipped out the man who had become the face of the campaign of terror conducted by both
CBP and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, Gregory Bovino, a buzzcut cliche of
a villain whose chief mission appeared to be the generation of “content”, specifically images
of himself strutting around Democrat-led cities like the general of an occupying army, right
down to the SS-style greatcoat.
Next, Trump subjected his homeland security secretary, the puppy-killing Kristi Noem, to an
emergency Oval Office meeting, from which his chief domestic policy adviser and the architect
of the anti-immigrant purge, Stephen Miller, was pointedly excluded. To complete the picture,
Trump spoke to Democratic leaders in Minnesota, later saying that he and they were now on
“a similar wavelength”.
That he felt compelled to make these moves is testament to the depth of revulsion prompted by
Pretti’s killing. Video footage, as well as the dead man’s biography, made a mockery of the
administration’s initial claims that Pretti was a “would-be assassin” bent on staging a
“massacre”. In Pretti, as with Renee Nicole Good, the armed agents of the state had picked the
wrong victim, someone Team Trump could not plausibly cast as “a domestic terrorist”, though
that didn’t stop them trying.
[Extracted with revisions and edits from “It is beyond naive for Democrats – and Europe – to
think Trump’s retreats are real. He never backs down for long”, The Guardian.]

content.passageText:
XVIII. Don’t be fooled. When it comes to Donald Trump, what might look like a full retreat
is almost always a mere tactical withdrawal, designed to buy time. He’ll step back when he’s
forced to, under pressure, but will then revert the instant the pressure lets up. Too often, his
opponents, whether at home or abroad, allow themselves to be played, confusing a mere pause
for a surrender – and the risk is strong that they’re making that same mistake all over again.
This week, the US president won praise in some quarters for moving to “de-escalate” the war
he has been waging on the people of Minneapolis. Following the killing of Alex Pretti, an
intensive care nurse who posed no threat and yet was shot at least 10 times by masked agents
of Customs and Border Protection or CBP, Trump signalled that he wanted to calm things down.
He shipped out the man who had become the face of the campaign of terror conducted by both
CBP and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, Gregory Bovino, a buzzcut cliche of
a villain whose chief mission appeared to be the generation of “content”, specifically images
of himself strutting around Democrat-led cities like the general of an occupying army, right
down to the SS-style greatcoat.
Next, Trump subjected his homeland security secretary, the puppy-killing Kristi Noem, to an
emergency Oval Office meeting, from which his chief domestic policy adviser and the architect
of the anti-immigrant purge, Stephen Miller, was pointedly excluded. To complete the picture,
Trump spoke to Democratic leaders in Minnesota, later saying that he and they were now on
“a similar wavelength”.
That he felt compelled to make these moves is testament to the depth of revulsion prompted by
Pretti’s killing. Video footage, as well as the dead man’s biography, made a mockery of the
administration’s initial claims that Pretti was a “would-be assassin” bent on staging a
“massacre”. In Pretti, as with Renee Nicole Good, the armed agents of the state had picked the
wrong victim, someone Team Trump could not plausibly cast as “a domestic terrorist”, though
that didn’t stop them trying.
[Extracted with revisions and edits from “It is beyond naive for Democrats – and Europe – to
think Trump’s retreats are real. He never backs down for long”, The Guardian.]

content.passageText:
XIX. Socialists claim that the “welfare” state alone has the merit of granting us social and
economic security, but such a security will not function permanently, and even if it could do
so, it would be as a long-term policy, both morally and socially undesirable. The political object
of security is to remove from the minds of the people the fear of unemployment.
Full employment, which is regarded as one of the aims of the Welfare State, is, in the final
analysis, a fraud. It is a farce because as soon as employment is created in one direction, it
creates unemployment in the other direction. This is what we find at present in our country, and
to add salt to the injury, our ministers, well-versed in making illogical and irresponsible
statements, tell us that their aim is to increase the welfare of the people, raise their standard of
life and give them complete freedom.
These are empty slogans which do not fill the stomach of the common man. “Welfare” is based
upon employment and employment is based upon production. What we find today more and
more people are thrown out of employment due to confiscatory patterns of taxation. Unless our
production increases, national income cannot increase, and unless national income rises the
welfare cannot increase. The Welfare State is the prime cause of reducing productivity of the
country. Coercion can always provide full employment, but what it cannot do is to provide us
with a civilized standard of living and the means to enjoy it in the free fresh air of freedom.
The real problem is not that there will be 11 millions of jobs by 1961 i.e. by the end of the
Second Five Year Plan, but how much shall we produce and what in consequence will be our
standard of life? The problem of distribution on which much stress is being laid today and for
which confiscatory taxation is imposed upon the people, rich and poor alike, is after all more
easily solved, the more there is to distribute. It is this truth that must prevail, if we, in India, are
to survive.
[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Welfare state is socially and economically a national
disaster: GN Lawande”, ThePrint.]

I. Bihar is India’s poorest large-sized state as well population composition. A data
journalism series published in these pages on the quantity, educational quality and caste
inequality of Bihar’s labour force — the share of population either working or looking for
a job — offers crucial insights on the labour market challenges facing Bihar. While the
state is a laggard in terms of share of overall working-age population (15-64 year-old), it
has the highest share of what can be described as young workers in the 15-29 age-group.
Almost all of the anecdotal evidence suggests that an overwhelming share of the younger
part of this labour force either wants a government job or migrates outside the state for
mostly better-paying blue-collar work. Migration and the endless wait for an elusive
government job has robbed Bihar of its most important comparative advantage — an
abundance of cheap unskilled workers. If employed well — this would take a concerted
intervention from both the State and markets — Bihar could do much better in improving
income generation in not just things such as manufacturing but also agricultural
production.


Doing this, however, would require a recalibration of educational priorities in the state.
Bihar’s labour force is poorly educated compared with the national average. It should
make a stronger pivot towards vocational education (without compromising on higher
education facilities) so that students do not limit their options to the elusive government
job. This could hold more promise if implemented well for women, given the huge
unutilised potential in labour intensive manufacturing sectors such as garments
manufacturing. For a state that was the epicentre for Mandal politics and is known for a


fusion of caste mobilisation on the promise of representation for almost four decades now,
it is revealing that almost all social groups are over-represented in agricultural
employment and under-represented in manufacturing and private services. Primacy of
politics around reservations, even if well-intentioned or even radical in a state with a
history of entrenched feudal oppression, has failed to unlock upward economic mobility
for the so-called subaltern. Bihar, given its demographic dividend, is crucial for India’s
future growth. Exploiting this potential will require an honest alignment of politics to the
labour market realities, not mere poll promises.

content.passageText:
II. I’m thinking about the mother in Tillie Olsen’s “I Stand Here Ironing.” The iron goes
back and forth, back and forth, and so do her thoughts, tallying up all the ways she was
and was not enough as a mother. When we read this story in a class I teach for mother
writers, we always talk about mom guilt, and how difficult it is to raise children in the
midst of fraught moments in history.


For the narrator in the story, it was the Great Depression and World War II. For us mother
writers who gathered this past Wednesday night in downtown Minneapolis, it is the
occupation of our city by federal ICE agents who are kidnapping and killing people in
broad daylight. When I found out that an ICE agent had shot Renee Good in the face just a
short drive from our home, I was pouring coffee and scrolling on my phone while my
three-year-old son raced cars on our living room couch five feet away. He called for me. I
set my phone down and pushed the tears off my face with shaking hands. I went to him.


Even as I did what I could, I felt that all-too-familiar guilt that mothers know so well, and
that mother, writer, and activist Tillie Olsen wrote about in her oft-anthologized 1956
story. “I will become engulfed in all I did or did not do, with what should have been and
what cannot be helped.” How could I not feel guilty for not doing more, when there are
mothers in my city whose children have been taken from them? Where, in this necessary
resistance and revolution, did I belong?


My own words wouldn’t come to me, so I borrowed others’. I started searching for
poems to pair with possible action items to print out and put in my Little Free
Library. Typing the poems made me feel better. While I cut them out, I read them aloud
to my son. Each time I finished one, he said, “Anulla poem.” Another poem. In the class I
teach, we read poems, essays, and stories by mothers from various time periods and
places. We write and we share our writing. We laugh and we cry. We heal. From our
voices and the voices of writers before us, we weave together a community of mothers
who raise their voices and inspire one another.


When I opened my car door to drive to class this week, I couldn’t help thinking about
Renee Good. About the prize-winning poem she wrote that was shared widely online after
her murder. About the image of her driver’s side door, the pocket overflowing with kids’
toys.

III. If it was happening to humans, you would call it genocide. The latest available census
data for Madhya Pradesh shows that it’s left with only 3052 donkeys, an awful 94%
decline since 1997. This ‘animalcide’, however, is not limited to one state or country. Two
major factors (urbanisation+mechanisation and Chinese traditional medicine market) are
severing the worldwide man-donkey relationship, which goes back 7000 years. That far
from grieving this loss, we are not even noticing it, reflects our fundamental alienation
from plants and animals, air and earth. To mourn is to begin to heal. And begin to do the
work of saving what we have been killing mindlessly.


It’s true that excepting regions like sub-Saharan Africa, socio-economic factors are
deleting donkeys’ traditional roles in agriculture and transport. Even if this was the only
explanation for the drastic shrinking of their population, it shows us to be a hideously


thankless species. How swiftly we are forgetting how deeply our ancestors – artisans to
merchants to administrators – depended on them. Until just a few generations ago they
powered the caravans that linked cities, and in more ancient stories they ferried our
prophets and gods. There’s a second, more unconscionable cruelty. Ejiao, or donkey hide
gelatine, is not new to traditional Chinese medicine and beauty products. But demand’s
shot up on the back of the country’s prosperity, a 2011 period drama, Empresses in the
Palace, and an ageing population. Even so, it wouldn’t be decimating donkey populations
across other countries if those were putting up meaningful defences.


A 2021 comparative analysis of donkey and mule populations by Stuart L Norris et al
finds that between 1997-2018 India’s decline at 74% has actually been worse than China’s
72%. One country’s actions seem active, the other’s passive. But the end result being the
same, obviously neither can take the moral high ground. And guess who’s taking it along
with the donkey? Poorer communities. Across the developing world, there are folk badly
hit by the sudden surge in donkey prices. Often, this translates into a painfully increased
workload for poor women and girls. Who cares, say the rest.

IV. Every inch of land is precious for holding the potential of generating employment. At
the same time, the environment matters - not only as a buffer against existential climate


change but also because unchecked development undermines assets intended to enhance
economic well-being. It is through this lens that one should look at NITI Aayog's new
report that proposes reducing the coastal regulation zone (CRZ) limit from 500 m to 200
m, aligning with global norms. This change aims to unlock 2,790 sq km of coastal land for
economic activities like tourism and infra development. The panel also recommends
lowering mandatory green cover requirements for industrial zones from 33% to 10% as in
Taiwan, Indonesia and Vietnam. But polluting industries would still need to maintain up
to 25% green cover based on a graded index.


The proposal to reduce the coastal buffer zone needs a careful relook, as coastal erosion
and increasing frequency of extreme rain and cyclone events - highlighted by IPCC
assessments - threaten low-lying cities and heighten vulnerability for densely populated,
low-income communities. In India, 113 coastal cities face the risk of submergence. With a
coastline exceeding 11,000 km and highly varied coastal geomorphology, a one-size-fits-
all approach is unfeasible. Industrial activity must rise. As will associated emissions. This
makes the existing higher green cover norm of 33-40% crucial as a natural carbon sink.
Simply aligning green cover requirements with countries like Vietnam isn't viable, given
India's distinct emissions profile.


India must grow, keeping climate and ecological risks in mind. It needs customised,
sustainable regulations that protect the environment without stifling industry and rapid
business growth.

V. Over 10 years after the landmark NALSA judgment — it recognised a “third gender”,
affirmed trans persons’ fundamental rights and the right to self-determination of gender
identity — and five years after the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Rules,
2020 came into effect, trans persons in India continue to face discrimination. On October
17, the Supreme Court pulled up the Centre and state governments for “brutishly”
reducing the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 and its corresponding
rules to “dead letters” and exhibiting “a grossly apathetic attitude towards the transgender
community”. Jane Kaushik, a transgender woman, petitioned the Court after allegedly
facing discrimination and the forceful termination of her employment at two private
schools in Uttar Pradesh and Gujarat in the span of a year. The SC bench hearing the
matter constituted an advisory committee to assess the implementation of the Trans Act
and recommend a “viable equal opportunity policy… to be introduced by the Union and
state governments” within three months of the draft’s submission. For establishments
lacking their own policies, the Centre’s policy will be enforceable.


The creation of a panel to operationalise protections guaranteed in law is a welcome step.
But it speaks of a larger failure — the lack of political will to ensure that transgender
citizens can live a life of dignity and equality as guaranteed by the Constitution and
affirmed by the SC. The NALSA judgment and the Trans Rules mandate protections
against discrimination in employment, medical care and education for transgender

VII. Israel and Iran represent two contrasting systems at the intersection of politics and
religion, shaping their domestic governance and regional policies. Israel is constitutionally
defined as a “Jewish and democratic state”, a hybrid identity that embeds religious


symbolism within a modern parliamentary democracy, while guaranteeing basic civil
liberties regardless of faith — a balance that continues to evolve in public law and policy.

Iran, in contrast, is an Islamic Republic governed by the principle of Velayat-e Faqih — the
Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist — enshrined in its 1979 constitution. Under this system,
the Supreme Leader, a senior Shia cleric selected by the Assembly of Experts, holds
ultimate authority over the executive, judiciary, military, and foreign policy, reflecting the
fusion of religious authority with political power.

These divergent frameworks shape each state’s worldview and policies. Israel anchors state
legitimacy to Jewish identity within democratic structures, while Iran’s theocratic republic
prioritises Shiite Islamic jurisprudence as a core source of law and governance. Their
ideological divide — amplified since the 1979 Iranian Revolution — underpins much of
the historic hostility between the two neighbours.

Source: Al-Jazeera

content.passageText:
X. The Indian Penal Code, 1860, meticulously constructs a framework of liability that
extends beyond the direct perpetrator of a crime, recognizing the grave danger posed by
collective criminality and preparatory acts. This is achieved primarily through the doctrines
of abetment, conspiracy, common intention, and common object, which together form the
bedrock of holding individuals accountable for crimes they facilitate, plan, or commit in
concert.


Abetment, under Sections 107 to 120, criminalizes the process of instigating, conspiring, or
intentionally aiding the commission of an offence. It is an inchoate crime, punishable even
if the abetted act does not occur, though the penalty escalates if it does. Distinct yet related
is the substantive offence of Criminal Conspiracy under Section 120A, which punishes the
very agreement between two or more persons to commit an illegal act or a legal act by
illegal means. The agreement itself constitutes the crime, marking a point where law
intervenes at the earliest stage of collective criminal planning.


When a crime is executed by a group, the IPC employs potent doctrines of joint liability.
Section 34 introduces the principle of ‘Common Intention.’ It requires a prior meeting of
minds—a pre-arranged plan—between two or more persons. When a criminal act is done
in furtherance of this shared intention, each person is liable as if they alone committed the
act. This is a rule of evidence that attributes constructive liability based on shared subjective
intent. In contrast, Section 149 operates in the context of an ‘Unlawful Assembly’ of five or
more persons with a ‘Common Object’ from among those specified in Section 141. Here, if
any member commits an offence in prosecution of this common object, every member is
vicariously liable. The focus shifts from a proven prior plan to membership in a group with
an inherently dangerous unlawful purpose.


In essence, while abetment and conspiracy address the roots of collusion before and during
crime formulation, Sections 34 and 149 address its fruition in group action. Prosecutors
often employ these sections in tandem, using Section 149 for mob violence and Section 34


for smaller groups with a proven shared plan, ensuring the legal net is cast wide enough to
hold all culpable parties accountable for their role in the collective criminal enterprise.

content.passageText:
XI. The foundation of the international legal order rests upon the binding force of
agreements between states, a concept enshrined in the ancient principle of pacta sunt
servanda. This Latin maxim, meaning "agreements must be kept," is the very bedrock of
treaty law, ensuring predictability, stability, and good faith in international relations. While
its spirit underpins all contractual diplomacy, its modern, definitive codification is found
not in historic peace treaties like the Paris Peace Treaty, nor in the Hague Conventions
governing the conduct of war, but in a dedicated framework for treaty law itself. The
principle is formally articulated in Article 26 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of
Treaties (1969), which states that every treaty in force is binding upon the parties and must
be performed by them in good faith. Even the UN Charter, in its Article 2, implicitly relies
on this principle for its authority, but the comprehensive legal formulation is the work of
the Vienna Convention.


However, the sanctity of treaties is not absolute. A higher tier of legal norms exists that
restricts what states may agree upon, even consensually. These are known as jus cogens, or
peremptory norms of general international law. These fundamental principles, from which
no derogation is permitted, are considered so essential to the international community that
they invalidate any treaty or agreement conflicting with them. The source of these norms is
not found in specific bilateral investment treaties or the resolutions of a political body like
the UN Security Council. While the International Court of Justice may identify and apply
them, it does not create them. Instead, jus cogens norms are derived from peremptory norms
of general international law, recognized by the international community of states as a whole.
Examples include the prohibitions on genocide, slavery, torture, and aggressive war. They
form an inderogable core of international law, representing its constitutional principles and
standing above the ordinary law of treaties governed by pacta sunt servanda. Together, these


two doctrines create a structured hierarchy: states are bound by their agreements, but never
by agreements that violate the conscience of the international community.

Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties
